At that time I did not have complete information. It is perhaps important to him in his area, and I should like to give the full answer now.
Search and rescue operations are controlled by the R.C.A.F., which has an interdepartmental advisory committee. The marine superintendent of our hydrographic service is a member of this committee.
A number of rescue control centres have been established throughout Canada, the ones in the coastal areas being of particular interest to the hydrographic service. All our ships report their positions to the rescue control centres daily if they are moving from place to place, and less frequently when they remain in one area. They are available, when called on by the search and rescue organization from their control centres, to carry out any necessary operations.

Speaker, we appreciate your generosity in this respect and will be quite brief. We in this group support the amendment because we consider it involves a matter of great importance and some urgency. We think that in Canada three basic policies are required if we are going to lay sound foundations for our over-all economic development. The first is a nation-wide policy of conservation. The second is a nation-wide fuel and power policy as outlined in the amendment moved by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis), and those two should be related to a national public investment policy. We believe that at this stage in our economic development there must be a policy that coordinates and correlates all these sources of energy within the country. If we are going to produce satisfactorily for the present, and conserve our natural resources for the future, we believe this type of policy is necessary to avoid duplication, to avoid waste, to promote efficiency and to make for a higher standard of living.
We believe in the conservation of energy; and in that connection I want to quote briefly from a document from the United States. This is the United States scientific conference on the conservation and utilization of resources. It is dated in the year 1940, and at page 273 of volume 3 I find this:
There should be a national fuel policy that will in the long-run make for a higher standard of living than would result in an unplanned exploitative economy. Firstly, a resource like water power which is constantly renewing itself should be used to the full. In Canada, for instance, only 25 per cent of water power resources have been developed although much of the undeveloped area is remote from population.
Secondly, short-reserve fuels like petroleum and natural gas should not be used where with reasonable economy long-reserve fuels like coal can be used. It is estimated, for instance, that coal reserves are from ten to twenty times as large as the reserves of all other fuels combined. According to U.S. Federal Power Commission data based on 1947 experience, coal is the most efficient fuel in terms of energy required for producing a kilowatt-hour. If petroleum or natural gas is used for a use like power generation, it will only mean that some time later it will be necessary to convert coal into liquid fuels at the cost of a loss of approximately 50 per cent of the energy in the fuel.
It goes on to deal with the necessity for a thorough study of the resources of power


-coal and water power, oil and gas, and their correlation in a national policy.
We believe now is the time for the government to consider a policy as proposed by this amendment. We talk about the tremendous power development on the Columbia, and other rivers in Canada. We talk about the new means of utilizing all our great coal resources, and we know that the government is considering seriously the distribution of gas and oil on a national scale.
In this connection I do wish to point out that, so far as over-all planning is concerned -and I am referring to over-all planning of the development of natural resources- Canada actually lags behind India at the present time, although we refer to India frequently as one of the underdeveloped countries of the world. India, although starting late in the game, has developed a very sound policy for the over-all development of its natural resources.
Before concluding I should like to read a paragraph from a booklet entitled "First Five-Year Plan", and it deals with India. In this book is found a recital of their five-year plan for the development of natural resources for the whole of India, as the result of a national policy in which the activities of the national government and the state governments are combined. These are the objectives of the policy, and I present them to the house as being closely related to the objectives of a policy which would be well worthy of consideration by this government. It says under the heading "Objectives":
The central objective of planning in India is to raise the standard of living of the people and to open to them opportunities for a richer and more varied life. Planning must, therefore, aim both at utilising more effectively the resources, human and material, available to the community so as to obtain from them a larger output of goods and services, and also at reducing inequalities of income, wealth and opportunity. A program aiming only at raising output might result in most of the increased wealth flowing into the hands of a few, leaving the mass of the people in their present state of poverty. It would thus fail to achieve wider social objectives. On the other hand, a mere redistribution of existing wealth would impair the well-being of certain sections of society without sensibly improving the lot of the rest. Our program must, therefore, be two-fold, leading at once to increased productivity and reduction of inequalities. These two sides of the program act and react on one another and it is a matter of delicate judgment to decide to what extent an immediate advance in one direction is compatible with advance in the other. While in the initial stages the accent of endeavour must be on increased production-because without this no advance is possible at all-our planning even in the initial stages should not be confined to stimulating economic activity within the existing social and economic framework. That framework itself has to be remoulded so as to secure progressively for all members of the community full employment, education, security against sickness and other disabilities and adequate income.

I submit that those are splendid objectives for a nation such as India; and the objectives, as outlined in this booklet, could well be considered by the government of Canada when it considers the amendment now before the house.
That is all I am going to say at this time. We were anxious to bring this matter to the attention of the house without delaying procedure for any considerable length of time. But we do urge the government to consider that the present time is appropriate to undertake the necessary planning of resources development in Canada-and the possibility of a national fuel and power policy for Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to go into any extended discussion of the purport of the amendment. But since it would appear that Your Honour is going to permit a vote on it, then I do wish to explain our position with respect to it.
In a case of this kind it is our duty to examine the resolution itself, and the words in which the request is framed. It is not for hon. members to guess what is in the minds of those who present the amendment, even though there might be a suggestion that the policies of the party to which the hon. member belongs may, in themselves, necessarily give an added meaning to the amendment.
As the amendment stands it calls for the formulation-and I should imagine that it was "formulation" rather than "formation" that was intended-of a national fuel and power policy for the general advantage of the people of Canada. That, in a few words, is what this means.
The fact that there has been a hint by the hon. member who has just spoken that it goes further than that is not adequate reason for our taking the position that this says more than it actually means. I cannot refrain, however, from pointing out that the situation in India and in Canada illustrates perhaps more clearly than anything else could illustrate the immense difference between the types of policy which are required to be employed in the two countries. India is a country much smaller in land area than Canada, but with a population of 400 million people. Here in Canada, in the third largest country in the world, we have 15 million people. There has not been a time since this country acquired the status of a nation in 1867 when there has been such general development of our resources, not only as a result of the initiative and energy of the people, but also because of new

It is not there.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Before the hon. member came in that was exactly what I said. I am pointing out that it is not there. I do this because of the not unnatural tendency of many people outside to say: We must examine the policies of the party which has put forward a certain resolution. I am looking at this simply as the wording appears. I want to make it clear, however, to anyone who might suggest that there is implicit in this resolution an acceptance of socialist doctrine, I believe that in this vibrant and vital country of ours there never was a time when there were more reasons for Canada resisting the crippling shackles of socialism. Nevertheless, this resolution does put into words the general proposals upon which we were in agreement the other day. I only wish to comment on the statement made by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) that in certain proposals which he was kind enough to describe as excellent proposals I had been dealing with subjects that were under provincial jurisdiction. I cannot agree with him in that.
Surely, at a time when we are allocating to the Department of Defence Production, and those departments for which it constructs so many things, nearly half of the total budget, directly or indirectly, there are ways that the federal government can well allocate greater industrial production to Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Newfoundland, Prince Edward Island, or the western provinces, which are directly and immediately interested in the increased production of coal.
Then again, there was the point I made that our immigration policy could provide the long-term answer to this by encouraging the settling of industrial communities near to the sources of fuel supply. The third point was the encouragement of our export business. Surely, that is entirely, or almost entirely, within federal jurisdiction.
Then, there was the question of the development of electricity from coal. I recognize -and I think, to an extent that sometimes has become tiresome in this house, I have emphasized over and over again-the jurisdiction of the provincial governments over the development of resources. Nevertheless,

National Fuel and Power Policy I have at the same time urged that in these cases where it requires the co-operation of the federal and the provincial authorities to bring them into operating form, the dominion government should not only be agreeable to doing this but should actually suggest a way in which it could be done.
Only within the past few months a development was opened in New Brunswick which called for co-operation between the federal and provincial governments in the development of electric power resources by the harnessing of the Saint John river. I have repeated my suggestion on different occasions that we should explore more vigorously than we ever have the possibility of using some of the Nova Scotia seams of coal and other of our bituminous coal for the production of electricity. I do not mean simply to encourage the use of coal in the furnaces of electric plants; I mean the actual burning of the coal below ground to produce the power sources, as I have actually seen done in Germany and in Russia. It has been done for years in a very efficient manner. It produces electric power at a price higher, it is true, than hydroelectric power but on a very satisfactory economic level. I am sure that is something which with the research facilities and the financial resources of the federal government could be carried out by mutual agreement and in co-operation with the provincial governments.
The fifth specific proposal I put forward was for the encouragement of the chemical uses of coal. There again it is a case of research by the national research council into the possibilities of the wider use of these very friable coals with a high chemical content. I have said it before, and I can only repeat it again, that I have seen in Europe a fantastic variety of things used in daily life made from the chemical by-products of coal. I believe there are opportunities in that field and that more could be done by the specific allocation of research tasks to the national research council for the encouragement of the coal industry in the areas where the quality of the coal itself sometimes makes it difficult to ship it over long distances. When I speak of quality I am not talking about the fuel content, but simply the fact that it is a very friable coal and in some cases does not lend itself to shipment over long distances as satisfactorily as anthracite coal.
I shall say no more, but I do not wish to leave the suggestion that the proposals I have made were outside the field of consideration of this government. I indicate that I shall support this motion. I do so with emphasis on the fact that we read into


it nothing that is not in the words. We accept no socialist doctrine that might perhaps be interpreted by others as an appropriate method of carrying this into effect. We simply accept the words as they are, and we do support the request that there be a national fuel and power policy which will be for the general advantage of the people of Canada, and particularly for the immediate solution of the very serious situation in Nova Scotia and in other areas where the coal industry is now so depressed.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to take just a minute to explain the position which my group is to take on this amendment. Like the Leader of the Opposition, I should like to emphasize that we take our stand on the basis of the amendment as it is worded, and certainly not with respect to any implications that there might be in the wording of it. We would not support it if it envisioned the establishment in Canada of a centrally planned economy that carried with it all the implications of a socialist economy.
I was just a little afraid that the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) was going to spoil it by bringing in too much of a five-year plan. I have no objection to five-year plans or ten-year plans excepting so far as they do set up a central planning board that tends to do the kind of thing that a good many private individuals and private interests are perfectly capable of doing, I think, much more capably. However, I do realize the necessity for having a more definite national fuel and power policy.
As a matter of fact, for a good many years spokesmen of our group in this house advocated that very thing. When the hon. member for Kootenay West says, "The time is now for the formulation of such a policy", I say the time is long past. There was a time when it would have been possible to save the coal industry, but at the moment it is a very difficult thing simply because we did nothing in years gone by to help to save it. We did not set up a national fuel policy that would bring about the optimum of cooperation between the provincial and federal governments and the full co-ordination of effort which would be demanded if a successful policy was to be established. I think the time is long past and I am afraid irreparable damage has been done.
We find in the province of Alberta today a terrific conflict between the producers of natural gas on the one hand and the producers of coal on the other. We could include with the producers of natural gas the producers of oil, which has become a very successful competitor of coal. How they are going to solve that in Alberta, where the conflict has taken

place on a large scale and to a certain degree, I do not know. It could have been solved years ago but it was not.
I think the government of Canada has been shortsighted in not understanding the situation in the provinces. They never really tried to understand the situation in Nova Scotia and they certainly have never tried to get down to a full understanding of the situation in Alberta. I recall hearing, when younger, a debate in the legislature of Alberta where a member representing a coal area advocated the export of coal. Another member representing a farming area threw up his hands in holy horror and said that if they did that it would not be very long before there would be no fuel left in the province and they would have to import it. The fact is that that sort of shortsighted attitude has been in existence for many years. As recently as three years ago the leader of the Liberal party in Alberta was taking exactly the same stand with respect to the export of gas. He brought himself into serious conflict with the interests of the federal Liberal party who were anxious to have the export of gas.
Our fuels have been bandied around for political purposes too long and it seems to me it is about time that an honest effort was made to get the co-operation of the provincial governments who are charged with the major responsibility for the development of resources. Having got that co-operation, I am satisfied it will be possible to set up a policy in specific terms to co-ordinate the efforts of all governments concerned so that our resources may be developed in the interests of the country.
The various factors involved have been dealt with by the Leader of the Opposition and it is not necessary for me to repeat them as I do not want to hold up the debate that long. The setting up of a national fuel and power policy should be one that would be fair and just to the various interests and sections of the country. In so far as it deals with related matters that fall within the jurisdiction of the federal government I propose to support the resolution and I am sure that members of this group will do likewise.

Mr. Speaker, I want to say to hon. members of the house that we are under no illusion. We know that we are living in a capitalist society and that a resolution of this sort would have to be put into effect in the kind of economic environment in which we live. It is true that we do not live in a democratically planned economy and when I hear it suggested that the planning of some phases of a planned economy introduces the shackles of socialism I wonder where the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) gets that idea.

I happened to be in Great Britain last year and I went down to Cardiff and the region where some of the most depressed areas of Britain were located. But for the planning that took place when the Labour party was in power, the great steel industry adjacent to Cardiff would not be providing employment in those formerly depressed areas. The same is true of Cumberland and many other parts of Great Britain. When I hear reference to the shackles of socialism I call to mind Norway, Sweden and Denmark where they have had socialist governments for many years and where the people are more unshackled than the people anywhere else in the world. I look back at the years 1930 to 1935 when there was no planning of any description and many of our people were shackled under a load of depression, misery and want. Our young people were wandering up and down the countryside. However, I am not going into that.
All I rose to say was that we are under no illusion. We know perfectly well that if this resolution passes it will have to be implemented in the economic environment in which we are living. We would support anything in the way of a fuel policy under the capitalist system under which we live or under a democratically planned economy under which we may live in years to come because we believe that such a policy is a sound one under any circumstances. I want to assure the Leader of the Opposition and the leader of the Social Credit group that when this resolution was formulated by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) he had no ulterior motive. It is in line with other resolutions which he has moved in the past. I wanted to say this in view of the manner in which the resolution has been received by the Leader of the Opposition and others.

If it means what the hon. member for Cape Breton South suggested before he read its terms, that is that the federal government should take over jurisdiction to deal with those aspects that are within the jurisdiction of the provinces, then that is something the government is not prepared to do at this time. It might be desirable in a unitary form of government but it is not the situation which results from the B.N.A. Act. If it means that the government should proceed to take steps to acquire the jurisdiction that is now the jurisdiction of the provinces, then this party will resist it, because that is not its policy. Because of the ambiguity of the terms and the various implications that can be put upon those terms, I feel, as far as I am concerned, that I have to vote against it. I cannot take the risk of voting for it by putting upon it the innocuous construction put upon it by the Leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for Peace River.
We all agree that these good things are good things, and we all agree that we should work together to make them beneficial to the Canadian people. But I cannot accept the suggestion of the hon. member for Peace River that we have not been farsighted because we did not try in advance to arrange something that would settle the conflict between the producers of coal and the producers of oil and the producers of gas in Alberta. Those are provincial resources, and they are resources that are competitive in their nature, but the way in which they are dealt with in the province is a provincial problem to be dealt with under the constitution by the provincial authorities.

That makes it impossible for us to accept any blame for having been shortsighted because we did not attempt to prescribe by legislation a solution for that problem that would have prevented the farmer member in the legislature of Alberta from making the speech he made and to which the hon. member for Peace River has referred. The question of whether or not in the exercise of our jurisdiction we are following the right path and moving along it fast enough for the best interest for the economic future of this country is precisely the reference made to this royal commission that is just about to enter upon its undertaking.
When that royal commission has reported, if it finds that there should be some deviation from the path we have followed, that will be considered. If it finds something more should be done so that there will be greater dispatch in achieving the objective, that also will be considered. However, for the time being I am sorry to have to say to the hon. member for Cape Breton South that we are not going to ask for a constitutional amendment to give us the powers he feels it would be desirable that we have to handle this situation in a more expeditious and, as he envisages it, a more effective way than is being done by the provinces.

Mr. Speaker, might I just say a few words in closing this? For the benefit of the Leader of the Opposition, the resolution means what it says. The principal item of interest is the $80,000 for the publication of a new consolidation of statutory orders and regulations. The last such consolidation, and the first one ever made, was published in 1950. It is now out of date both in substance and in form; in substance because of many amendments to and revisions of regulations that have been made since that time, in form because the statutes themselves were revised in 1952. The government has consequently decided that a new consolidation would now be worth the fairly substantial cost that it necessarily involves.
The new consolidation will conform in its arrangement to the new revised statutes. It will contain all regulations in effect at January 1, 1955, with the exception of those exempt from publication under the Regulations Act and some voluminous regulations, such as those made by the board of transport commissioners, which are published by those who make or administer them. I should add by way of explanation that among the regulations exempt from general publication are a great many that apply only to members of the public service and the armed services, and these are of course circulated directly to those affected by them and are available of course to members of the house and to the press should they wish to see them.
The new consolidation has been used as the occasion for making a fairly comprehensive revision of outstanding regulations, not only to incorporate previous amendments but to improve them both in form and in substance.
We have taken a number of measures to reduce the size and expense of the new consolidation. Many lengthy forms and technical appendices, which can be readily obtained by those who need them, are merely described and not reprinted in the consolidation. The number of cross-references in the text has been reduced, but a full index retained. The individual volumes will be larger, about 1,200 pages as compared with 900 in the 1950 volumes, but there will be only three instead of five, that is to say, about 3,600 pages instead of the 4,500 that were in the former consolidation. Fewer copies will be printed, and there will be less free distribution. By this means we hope to reduce the cost of printing in the two languages from the $103,000 that it was in 1950 to 
about $80,000 which we feel should be sufficient to cover the cost in spite of increases in the cost of printing.
Despite these economies, I am still concerned with the high cost of producing periodical consolidations of this kind. I have asked that a detailed study be made of alternative arrangements that would provide a convenient and authoritative source of reference at less cost. But, of course, in this day and age parliament must necessarily delegate to the government and to ministers the making of detailed regulations to carry into effect the statutes that are passed. That being so, I think we owe it as a duty to those who are affected by these statutes and regulations, as well as to those who elect us, to make these laws and regulations readily accessible to those they concern. We cannot shirk this duty because of the cost that it involves but we must ensure that it is discharged as economically as possible. Hon. members of the committee will of course have an opportunity of examining our new consolidation in whatever detail each may desire, and I wish to assure all members of the house that we will welcome any suggestions any member may wish to make designed to make the consolidation more convenient for ready reference and make it easier to have the regulations known and properly carried out.
I would hope it would appeal to members of the committee to confirm this appropriation and thereby indicate that they feel this is really a necessary document to have available to those who have to administer the regulations and to those who are affected by the regulations.

Mr. Chairman, under this department we have the salary of the Prime Minister, and there is a matter I should like to draw to his attention. It has often been said that the Prime Minister opens the house and the opposition closes it. I am not going to discuss the matter of the opposition closing the House of Commons, but I am certain that the Prime Minister actually opens the house. I should like to suggest to the Prime Minister that consideration be given as to future policy with respect to sittings of the House of Commons. May I say that I am speaking personally and not on behalf of the group to which I have the honour to belong.
During the present session, with the exception of the short recess at Easter, the House of Commons will have been in session approximately seven months. I am convinced that as Canada grows, and Canada is going to grow, the work and responsibility of government and the work and responsibility of the House of Commons and the

6SS9
Senate are also going to increase. Although a number of alterations have been made in the rules of procedure of the house which are to come into effect at the next session,
I prophesy that over the years the length of sessions each year is going to be extended and not reduced. That being so, I should like to ask the Prime Minister to give very serious consideration to the times of meeting of the House of Commons. I do not think it is in the best interests of doing the business of the people in the most beneficial and expeditious manner to hold continuous sessions. It is, I think, quite acceptable to members from Quebec and from Ontario and, to a certain extent, the members who represent their constituencies in adjacent provinces. But, sir, Canada is a land thousands of miles across, and I believe consideration must also be given to the position of members of the House of Commons who come from provinces far removed from Ottawa. I refer of course in particular to the maritime provinces on the Pacific and Atlantic coasts, and I would also include Alberta and Saskatchewan.
It is important that a member in the House of Commons be able to be in contact personally at times with his constituents and, I may say, to be in contact with his own family. I do believe greater consideration must be given to the fact that Canada is one nation, and that British Columbia, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Newfoundland have some rights that must be considered.
I understand that what I have suggested might not be possible of fulfilment at the next session; but I do suggest some thought be given to refraining from holding continuous sessions of parliament lasting for seven months-and I believe the sessions will be even longer as Canada develops. Recognition must be given to members coming long distances. I suggest the house might meet the last week of October or the first in November. It might sit until the middle or the third week of December and then be adjourned until the second week of January, to meet continuously from then forward until the completion of its business. In view of the size of this country and the responsibilities of all hon. members, I suggest this is a logical and reasonable request.
I am not placing my remarks on a personal basis; but I know that in order to be here on time I had to leave my home on January 1. With the exception of a few short days at Easter, I have not been home since that time to visit either my family or my constituents. I realize my family is my own responsibility, but my constituents are my House of Commons responsibility. Surely members from outside Ontario and Quebec, 50433-436*

I am certain the Prime Minister will give thought to this matter. He must recognize that as Canada develops sittings of both houses of parliament are going to be extended, rather than reduced. If this does not meet with the acquiescence of the Prime Minister, who has the responsibility of calling parliament together, then I make the suggestion that members who come from far-away provinces-and I am not going to define those provinces by any limitation such as 500 miles or perhaps a thousand miles-and who cannot get home during week ends, or even once a month, in the interests of our parliamentary democracy and of equal rights for members coming from long distances and having the same responsibility as, for instance, representatives from Ottawa, should be given, on a definite and responsible basis, opportunities for air transportation. speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as there have been some interesting developments in the activities which the federal district commission is undertaking, I thought it would be worth while to take a few minutes, even at this time, to make a short statement about these and to acquaint hon. members with some of the questions and problems confronting us in the development of our national capital. This information may be of some use to members and others in preparing for the joint committee of both houses which we propose to set up next year to study the various questions relating to the development of the national capital and the arrangements with Ottawa and the other municipalities in the area.
Parliament has already recognized the importance of creating a national capital which will be a source of legitimate pride and inspiration to all Canadians, a sort of focus and symbol of those ties which now unite us as a young but already quite vigorous nation. The recognition of this importance of the capital has been tangibly demonstrated by the action parliament has taken in establishing the federal district commission and placing at its disposal the resources necessary to develop, in co-operation with others, the physical aspects of our capital in keeping with the role that most Canadians wish it to play in our national life.
Until recent years, these activities of the commission were on a relatively small scale. In the past ten years we have developed a major long-term plan for this work, and have carried forward the implementation of that plan on a scale that greatly exceeds what was done in earlier periods. In this respect, as in so many others, we have seen a quickening in the pace of our national development. Under the vigorous leadership and

direction of the enlarged commission authorized by parliament in 1946, the excellent plans developed by Mr. Greber, Mr. Fiset and the late Mr. Kitchen, and their staffs and collaborators, have been carried some distance into execution. In the development of this plan, the commission has had the valuable assistance of the national planning committee. To this development, our other public works in Ottawa have also contributed, for the buildings undertaken by the Minister of Public Works and his department, and in some cases by other government agencies and departments, have been sited and designed to accord with and implement the plan for the national capital.
It has not been easy to distinguish those features of the plan and its execution which are peculiar to the national capital as such, and those which are simply appropriate to a modern North American city of the size and prosperity of Ottawa. Any city of this size and wealth should have a plan, and it should be developed in a manner that is sensible and yet as beautiful as circumstances and the length of its purse will permit. The commission itself, charged with the special responsibility for developing the national capital as such, and zealous to discharge those responsibilities in a manner and degree worthy of the trust parliament has shown it, has naturally taken the initiative, not only in the planning, but also in promoting the works necessary to implement the plan. It has been necessary for the government to examine carefully the projects of the commission to ensure that they fall within the proper sphere of responsibilities of the federal government, rather than the normal responsibilities of the city and of the province, and that they fit into the pattern of policy in accordance with which parliament established the commission and voted funds to carry out its program.
In recent years, the importance of a careful distinction between the functions of the city and of the federal authorities has been increased by the introduction of the Municipal Grants Act, and now by its revision at this session of parliament. Under the revised act, we shall be paying to the city of Ottawa the equivalent of full taxes on all our property in Ottawa which is in excess of the 2 per cent which is taken as a minimum measure of what federal property is normally to be found in any major municipalities. Given these grants, there is no reason for regarding the activities of the federal district commission in the planning and creation of a national capital as being in any way a substitute for the payment of full taxes to the city.
Supply-Privy Council
I would suggest, therefore, that one of the subjects to which our parliamentary committee should give attention next year is the proper definition of the type of project which should be carried out by the commission, and what should be expected of the municipality and perhaps of the provincial authorities. I say the "provincial authorities" because the capital area comprises both sides of the Ottawa river. Should it be necessary, in order to have a proper capital, that the federal authorities undertake work that should be undertaken by the municipality itself, the committee may wish to consider an extension of the practice that we have followed in the past under which adjustments would be made in the grant paid to the city under the Municipal Grants Act to take into account such work done by the commission as would normally be done at the expense of the municipality, just as adjustments have been made in the past in respect of such things as parks and the police services rendered by the R.C.M.P. in connection with the parks and parkways.
There is another general problem to which I would hope the members of this house and those who are on the joint parliamentary committee next session will give some study. This is one which is inherent in the planning and control of land use to achieve any longterm community program. We keep running into situations in the national capital area where not only the planning of land use is required, but also some measure of control if the best results are to be achieved over a long term, and if the most is to be made of the opportunities created by public actions and expenditures. In these circumstances, we find ourselves frequently met with the suggestion that the federal district commission or the government should acquire land in order to control its use. Some examples include property adjoining the driveways that have been created; properties adjoining those to be acquired from the railways in exchange for new properties south of Ottawa for the establishment of the freight yards; properties adjoining streets to the improvement of which the commission has contributed; and finally, properties in the areas which have been proposed as a green belt around the cities comprising the national capital. A serious potential problem has arisen by the need to construct new permanent headquarters for the Department of National Defence on the periphery of Ottawa and its environs. For several reasons this large headquarters can hardly be accommodated properly either in the downtown areas or elsewhere within the presently built-up areas of the city. If it
6S02

Supply-Privy Council is not to create new problems in the neighbourhood of its new location, some proper planning and control of the land use around it seems necessary.
These situations which I have described and illustrated all require some zoning and control. It seems to us to be inappropriate that the federal government should undertake this function, even in the capital area. It belongs more appropriately to the provinces and the municipalities to whom our constitution and traditions give jurisdiction in these matters. But this government hopes that these local responsibilities will be effectively discharged. With the approval of parliament and on behalf of the people of Canada we have assumed some responsibility for the proper development of the capital area. Canada is much the largest owner of land in the area. It is the principal employer. It now provides a large share of the revenue of the municipalities. Yet it has no vote or voice in municipal affairs. We must depend upon the sense of responsibility and good judgment of the provincial and municipal authorities in dealing with this problem. We wish to work in harmony with the local authorities and not at cross-purposes with them, nor do we wish to replace them in their proper role.
I think our committee should also have in mind that the municipal authorities here, in receiving the quite substantial grant now made under the Municipal Grants Act, have an obligation to this parliament as well as to others to undertake the zoning and control of land use in an effective way to promote the long-term interests of this community.
We are proposing to take one step now within our own powers and responsibilities. Hon. members will recall that the plan for the national capital included a green belt around the built-up areas of the national capital, in which it was proposed that the land would be used in a manner that would preserve some open space and rural appearance. This green belt is an important part of the plan which was drawn up by Mr. Greber and his associates, approved by the federal district commission, tabled in this house in April, 1949 and used as the basis of our plans in developing the capital. The basic idea was also set out in a report dated December, 1947 by the Ottawa planning area board set up under the legislation of the province of Ontario. This report was approved in principle by the municipalities affected and was acknowledged by the minister of planning and development of Ontario.
Neither this nor other proposals for the green belt have ever been fully adopted and given proper legal status, however. Recently, a decision by the Ontario municipal board

made clear that until the plan relating to the green belt had full legal status it would not be possible to prevent urban development within it. If such development is now facilitated in any way it will defeat the purpose of this aspect of our capital planning. I hope that the provincial and local authorities will co-operate in preserving a green belt about the capital and promote good planning and urban development in this respect. Nevertheless, we must await further action by the municipalities and the provinces concerned and cannot achieve our objective by federal action alone.
In the meantime, however, I believe that this house would not wish any action to be taken by agencies of the federal government that would be other than in harmony with the plan for a worthy capital which we are endeavouring to implement. One federal agency that has some responsibilities in this field is the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation which, of course, co-operates in financing and facilitating housing and land assembly and development for housing purposes.
The Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation are being directed immediately to restrict the facilities they provide under the housing act within the area of the green belt of the national capital. For the time being that belt will be defined for this purpose as the one in the plan of the Ottawa planning area board, dated December 1947, and acknowledged by the minister of planning and development of Ontario early in 1948. Its exact boundaries in so far as the housing act is concerned may from time to time be amended by consultation between the provincial and federal authorities concerned, in the light of further study.
The limitation to be imposed is that until further notice no assistance with respect to housing or land development in the designated area will be entertained by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation unless the proposed development is in accordance with a plan that has been approved under the Ontario planning act. I am sure that there will be general agreement that this is the best way to avoid a sporadic development which the government should not in any case underwrite and which should not be facilitated in contravention of the plan developed for our national capital.
I should make clear, however, that this negative action in respect of housing is by no means enough. Some positive action for the control of land use in the green belt will be required if it is to be properly maintained in the manner that has been proposed.
I would point out for the consideration of our parliamentary committee, however, that

this maintenance of a green belt will pose a major financial problem that cannot be overlooked. It will require a restriction on the use of land that will prevent its sale or use for purposes that might be more valuable financially than those to which it is restricted. This restriction is in the public interest, but it is not in the interest of the individual owner. A problem of compensation arises.
The principles involved in this question are, however, very complicated and controversial. I am informed that there is relatively little agreement on them by authorities in this field, let alone any simple means of implementing such principles in respect of the federal capital of a country like this. The value of such land for development purposes arises from the growth of the community and from various actions taken by public authorities, rather than to any large extent from action on the part of owners themselves. But the owners of other land outside the restricted areas are normally subject to much less stringent zoning restrictions and are consequently free to make profits from the development of their land. Moreover, it is not certain that any one parcel in any area within or without the green belt would in fact be used for development at any particular time. Most of it would not be used until much later at any rate. It would be unfair to the taxpayers at large, of whatever authority is involved, to make compensation to all owners of land for this element of what is called "floating value" considering the fact that some parcels might be saleable for development purposes.
In regard to this particular case of a green belt around the municipalities comprising the national capital, I think the committee should consider whether the federal government ought to share with the provincial authorities and the municipalities concerned in the cost of whatever compensation it might be fair to make.

May I interrupt the Prime Minister, as it is one o'clock. I was wondering if he had very much more. I am not thinking of the members of the committee but of the members of the staff who were working until after four o'clock this morning. If there is very much more I would suggest that the Prime Minister resume at half past two.
