speechtext: On item 340.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when we broke off for lunch I was mentioning the problem of whether or not it would be fair that there be some compensation to owners of land within the green belt because of the restrictions that might be put on the use of that land. I was suggesting that the committee of the houses of parliament to be set up next year consider that problem. If they came to the conclusion that there should be some compensation, they should consider whether the federal government should participate in any way with the province and municipalities in making fair provision for such owners whose rights to use their land might be restricted in the general interests of the community.
It would be desirable, I think, to relate any action in that regard to a general policy

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
Supply-Privy Council to be followed by the provincial authorities in regard to the planning, control and betterment of land use in general. I hope that the creation of a proper green belt around the capital will not be prevented or unduly delayed by lack of action on the part of those concerned in addition to the federal authorities. I think this government and parliament would be ready to join with others in seeking an effective and fair means of implementing this important element of the over-all plan.
Now I should like to turn briefly to some other aspects of federal district commission activities and plans. I should say first that the legislation establishing the federal district commission itself appears to need some moderate revision, and we plan to bring in an amending bill as soon as convenient following consideration of the subject by the joint committee. This would relate to such things as the organization, powers and procedures of the commission itself, the legal delineation of the national capital area, the revision of the statutory grant made to the commission, which for some years has had to be supplemented by an appropriation, and other matters that may arise out of the consideration of the whole subject by the joint committee.
It may well be that the committee will feel that, instead of having a statutory grant, the whole appropriation required for upkeep purposes should be subject to annual consideration by parliament. Those are matters about which it will be, I think, in the public interest to have a considered opinion expressed by this joint committee.
I should say, secondly, in regard to the operations of the commission, that it has now become part of our regular, continuing machinery of government. It has devolved a long way from the old Ottawa improvement commission, which undertook the creation of parks and parkways. It has, nevertheless, the same basic purpose and spirit, and it is largely the scale and continuity of its operations that have changed.
The commission now has an annual maintenance budget of approximately $1J million and a capital budget of several million dollars a year. It has 350 full-time employees and it hires between 100 and 200 men for seasonal work during the spring and summer months. I think lion, members would be as interested as I was to visit the headquarters of the commission at 291 Carling avenue. That is where the work of the commission is carried out. I was very much interested to see that they have the plans and sketches kept continuously up to date with the projections for the future, and I felt well rewarded for the time I took. I had

to take it before nine in the morning because these days from nine in the morning till eleven at night there is not much opportunity to do anything else than attend to one's parliamentary duties. But I felt well rewarded for the time I spent there seeing what the set-up was, how the plans were being kept up to date, and what work was being done by the staff. They are organized under the management of the general manager who is responsible to the commission itself.
The members of the commission, as hon. members know, serve without remuneration, and they meet normally from six to eight times a year. In recent years it has become necessary for the chairman to devote much more of his time to the work of the commission. I think it desirable that the chairman's position should not be a full-time job, but I think in future we will have to recognize that it demands more than can be expected from an active busy man without any compensation, as the statute now provides.
The present chairman of the commission, as hon. members know, is Mr. Howard Kennedy. It so happens that he is under retainer from the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources as a consultant on forestry matters, because he is recognized as one of the most competent forest authorities in this country. He is also the federal member of the eastern slopes of the rockies federal-provincial commission. The retainer he has from the department of northern affairs is not just a formality. He is very frequently consulted by the officers of that department, and the reason for the retainer did have also in its motivation the fact that, if he were not receiving that retainer here, he would be doing much more work outside of Ottawa and would not be available for the work he is doing for the federal district commission. The retaining fee I understand that he has from the department is $6,000 and his remuneration as the federal member of the eastern slopes of the rockies commission is $3,500.
In speaking of maintenance operations of the commission I should explain the rather complicated arrangement of its finances. It derives its funds for maintenance from three sources and its money for capital expenditures and for payments to municipalities for assistance in construction projects from the national capital fund.
The three sources of revenues for maintenance are first the statutory grant of $300,000 a year provided under the Federal District Commission Act. This is now much less than the cost of maintaining even the parks and

parkways which are the statutory responsibility of the commission. This maintenance cost now amounts to about $750,000 a year and is gradually increasing as the size of these properties increases.
The second source of funds is the revenue of the federal district commission itself. It is a corporate entity and receives revenues of several types. Some substantial portion of it comes from service rendered to government departments for which payment is made by those departments. Some of it comes from the sale of certain nursery products that it provides to others. Some of it comes from the rental of properties owned by the commission as an agent of the crown. Hon. members will notice that in the estimates there is a nominal vote, No. 340, to make clear the authority of the commission to expend those funds that come in as revenue. There was some doubt in the Auditor General's mind as to whether those revenues that are derived from the property under its control could be expended, so it was thought desirable to have a nominal vote in the estimates to make it clear that although they have to account for these funds, they can form part of what they spend for the maintenance of the properties entrusted to them.
The third source of revenue is the annual appropriation for maintenance work. This is vote 341 of the privy council estimates. The bulk of this vote is to enable the commission to defray the cost of maintenance of grounds adjoining government buildings in Ottawa. It was felt that it would not be good economy to have two authorities dealing with the maintenance and the landscaping of lands that either belong to the government directly or are under the control of the federal district commission, and that it would be better to have one authority doing the whole of the same kind of work that is required. This vote also provides-as it has provided for several years-additional funds to supplement the statutory grant to make possible the maintenance of the parks and parkways in the care of the commission. For the current fiscal year the statutory grant is $300,000. The amount of revenue expected to be used for maintenance expenditures is $413,827. Perhaps this is a rather precise figure, but that is the calculation made by the officers of the federal district commission. The amount to be voted under item No. 341 is $622,105 which, it will be noted, is held at the same figure as was in the estimates last year. Thus the total expenditures on administration, construction, operation and maintenance will be, we expect, $1,335,932. That is the figure for which we are requesting an appropriation.
Supply-Privy Council
This total will be divided into four main categories of expenditures. In view of the corporate nature of the federal district commission, those are not shown in detail in the estimates book but I thought they would be of interest to the house. About $109,000 of the total is for the administration of the commission itself and its central office, including the travelling expenses of the commissioners, the majority of whom, I may say, reside outside of Ottawa. About $750,000 of the total is, as I have said, for the maintenance of parks and parkways, the property which is held by the commission on behalf of the crown. There is about $365,000 for the maintenance of properties adjoining government buildings in Ottawa. We use the federal district commission to do this outdoor work on these grounds as well as on its own for reasons I mentioned a moment ago. This work ranges from the planting of, I would say, the magnificent flower beds here in front of the parliament buildings to the mowing of the lawns or the grass around even the lowliest of our laboratories. Finally, we have the direct cost of the planning of the national capital, about $113,000, which includes the expenses of the national capital planning committee and its information office. This information office provides and keeps up to date the model of the national capital and the other material illustrating the national capital plan and the various stages of its implementation.
I turn now to what is perhaps the more interesting aspect of the commission's work, namely its capital projects. I have mentioned that they are financed from the national capital fund which was set up in 1948. There have been seven instalments of $2| million each put into that fund and we are asking parliament to appropriate the eighth instalment, making in all $20 million.
Expenditures from the fund to the end of the last fiscal year were $13,019,824, leaving a balance in the fund of $4,480,176 as at March 31, 1955. If the eighth instalment is paid, this amount will be increased by another $2J million. This balance includes both the moneys advanced and still held by the commission and the remainder which is held in trust by the treasury pending its advance to the commission. Expenditures from the fund last year were $5,508,955 or more than twice the expenditures of the preceding year. This high level of expenditure was due mainly to the purchases of property in and around Ottawa and Hull and, second, to construction projects, notably the railway cut-off south of Ottawa, the building of Sussex drive in Ottawa to which the commission contributed,

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Supply-Privy Council and the building of parkways on the Quebec side of the capital area. Details of these expenditures will, of course, appear in due course in the commission's report which was tabled early in January in this house. The details are also in volume II of the public accounts. Expenditures for the preceding year and the total up to that time will be found at pages 41 and 42 of volume II of last year's public accounts.
For the current fiscal year the expenditures planned for the fund, if parliament approves this further contribution, are budgeted at $8,134,000. Of this total, $2,550,000 is for the purchase of land, and nearly all the balance, namely $3,279,000, is for construction, either directly or by grants toward the cost of municipal construction projects. Sometimes the commission makes, with the approval of the governor in council, a grant to forestall the time when the municipality would be doing the work if it were not for the implementation of the federal district plan. I will not endeavour to go into the details of the capital budget. They are shown in the budget which was tabled here on the 23rd of June.
I would, however, like to mention the status of some of these major projects. The largest project, of course, and, indeed, the key feature of the whole plan is the relocation of the railways. The federal district commission has purchased land in the southeastern part of Ottawa to provide eventually for railway lines and yards there in place of those which are within the city itself. On this property it has now constructed a cut-off for freight trains, which has already made it possible to abandon the old cross-town tracks of the C.N.R. to the west of where they cross Carling avenue. They will be abandoned farther east as the property is needed for the expressway. The plan is that only some two tracks and certain sidings will be retained for some years pending the time when the whole railway network may be moved to the south of the city.
The new freight yards south of the Walkley road and the various associated facilities will be finished during the next few months and will make possible the transfer this summer, we think, of most of the freight movement from the present Bank street yard of the C.N.R. in the centre of the city.
The next step in our railway program is the working out of arrangements for a jointly operated railway terminal area for Ottawa that will include both freight and passenger operations. This is being actively pursued now by the federal district commission with the two railways, and with the help of the services of a firm of specialized consulting

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
engineers in planning the new railway facilities. Once agreement on these arrangements has been reached, we plan over the next few years to remove the C.N.R. freight terminal from its present position near the station to the Hurdmans Bridge area, and to eliminate the C.P.R. Sussex street branch south of St. Patrick street. We also plan to improve the union station arrangements and in five or six years' time perhaps to eliminate the railway line across the interprovincial bridge to Hull, using instead the bridge at Nepean bay.
It is hoped that within the next five or six years the whole complex of lines across the Rideau river at Hurdmans Bridge, and crossing the canal at Pretoria and turning down to the station can be elevated sufficiently to facilitate crossing all the important roads and streets in this area without level crossings while preserving the appearance of the capital. As time goes on, it is hoped to move more and more of the freight yards to the south and east of the city.
From this movement of the railways we can expect important positive benefits. The government has offered the cross-town right-of-way formerly used by the C.N.R. to the city and the province as a right-of-way for a modern limited access expressway across the city from east to west. When I say "limited access" I mean limited access from within the city. The federal district commission has been acquiring and is continuing to acquire property to complete the right-of-way to the necessary width for the expressway, although it is not proposed that we should undertake to provide all the property that is needed for ramps and connections with intersecting streets. We think that part should be left to the responsibility of the civic authorities inasmuch as it is more particularly of immediate limited local concern.
We feel that this is much the best use for the land in terms of the national capital plan. It provides a wonderful opportunity for the city to secure a modern traffic artery where and when it will be needed. It is not to be a parkway. It will be a main commercial traffic artery in and out of the capital city and across it. If the province wishes, the federal government is prepared to have this designated as part of the transcontinental highway, though it will be within the city limits, and thus eligible for a grant from the federal crown on the basis of its being part of the transcontinental highway. Otherwise, however, the federal government will not contribute to the construction costs. We believe that the contribution of the property of the land, the right-of-way, which is estimated to be worth at least $5 million or

somewhat more, is a fair share for the federal authorities in a project which, after all, is in large part one that might perhaps be considered a normal part of the programs of both the city and the province.
I will not endeavour to go into any construction details about this major project. Hon. members who are interested will find considerable information about it in the Smith report on the traffic plan for Ottawa, which I got leave to lay on the table this morning so that it might be available for these who might wish to consult it.
I should also mention the completion of Sussex drive and the bridges on it across the Rideau river. To this project the federal district commission has contributed about two-thirds of the cost and the city and the province the remainder. This will, I think, be a valuable supplement to the driveway and parkway network of the federal district commission itself, and it provides a suitable location for many federal buildings, some of which are already built alongside it. The design of the driveway itself and the boulevard in the centre of it have given rise to some questions, and in this connection the federal district commission cannot avoid some responsibility. It was consulted and it approved of the plans as they were carried out. I am informed that the width of the boulevard strip and' the nature of the entrances are in accord with good modern practice in such matters. But I drive through there more than once a day, and now that there is no longer any question of lawsuits over the very unfortunate accident that cost the life of a constable on the very day that the driveway was opened, I hope that some consideration will be given to easing a bit the angles as you come off the bridge into the rest of the driveway.
There was another matter that was giving me some concern. There was a turn from the driveway to go down into Lady Grey parkway. I thought that was pretty inconvenient and I inquired to find out who was responsible for relocating the entrance to Lady Grey drive across a bit of park land opposite the premises occupied by the Franciscan Fathers. I found that little bit of land belonged to the federal district commission and it was the body which was providing the alternative entrance into Lady Grey drive. Perhaps it should have been done in the first place but I am glad to see it is being done now. It will be possible to have one-way entrances and exits from Lady Grey drive and thus avoid the possibility of accidents that the planners originally
Supply-Privy Council wished to avoid by making it necessary to go so slowly that accidents would not be apt to happen.
One of the major projects for the coming year is the reconstruction of the approaches to the old Chaudiere bridge across the Ottawa river, particularly on the Hull side. This project will enable this old federal structure and its approaches to accommodate safely the modern traffic load that is using it. As part of the project, the old streetcar route over the bridge has been replaced with buses. This replacement permits the tracks to be removed from Wellington street west of Bank street, on which, as hon. members know, many of our finest government buildings are situated. With the completion of this project and Sussex drive we shall have completed most of the driveway projects planned for the present decade on the Ottawa side of the capital area. Finances permitting, we plan to proceed with the acquisition of property on which to build parkways in the 1960's or later, as economic conditions permit. Of course capital planning is a field where we must take a long-term view.
Most of the actual construction of driveways over the next several years will be on the Quebec side of the river. The most immediate will be further work on the Lac des Fees parkway in Hull proper, on which the commission plans to complete the grading and gravel base this year. It is also proceeding this year with construction of a part of the Gatineau parkways which is intended to open up to visitors to the capital some of the beautiful park land that has been acquired in the Gatineau hills to provide a natural background-perhaps a quite unusual background-for the capital itself. For several years construction of this parkway has been delayed because of difficulties in acquiring the land at reasonable cost. The present year's program is confined to a portion of road that can usefully be built on property already owned by the crown.
In the Gatineau hills we have now a beautiful natural park. It is being enjoyed, I am told, by many tens of thousands of visitors each year, as well as very frequently by large numbers of the people of Ottawa and Hull. It is planned in due course to round it out by acquiring more land in the area designated for the park in the national capital plan. There seems to be no particular hurry in this matter, however, and we do not see any necessity for using expropriation processes to secure property which is being used in a manner that does not detract from the park we have already formed. And we do not think we need to pay high prices or

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Supply-Privy Council prices higher than are considered to be proper market prices, for the acquisition of land by negotiated agreements.
I shall not endeavour to go further into detail about what the commission has accomplished and is doing. Much is available in the annual reports of the commission, and the financial details of its current plans are in the budget already presented to parliament.
I hope that early during the next session hon. members will have a chance to study what is being done and what is being planned, and I hope they will use this opportunity to help further the development of a capital of which probably a much more populous nation of the future will be proud.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to make any extended remarks in regard to the survey that has been presented to us by the Prime Minister in connection with the capital plan. I do think it is unfortunate that a joint committee of both houses did not proceed with a consideration of this subject during the session that is now coming to a close. The Prime Minister has said that this will be done at the next session, and I trust it will be proceeded with immediately after the new session opens.
I hope however that it will not be within the confines of the wording appearing in the speech from the throne this year, because the reference made on that occasion, on January 7, said that-
A joint committee of both houses will be proposed to examine, in the light of the Municipal Grants Act and possible amendments thereto, the financial and other relationships of the government and the federal district commission with the city of Ottawa and neighbouring municipalities.
I do not think that such a committee should have any such limitations, nor do I think it wise that it should even have these terms of reference. They suggest that there is some implied condition arising between municipal grants and the attitude of the federal government toward the course of action followed by municipalities. Certainly I do not think there should be any suggestion that municipal grants in lieu of taxes carry with them any obligation to submit the activities of any municipality to the supervision of the federal government.
The situation so far as the capital plan is concerned is, of course, something entirely different, and I think for that reason that the reference to municipal grants is unnecessary, because it could mislead the members of the committee, as well as members generally in the House of Commons, as to the real purpose of the committee itself.
I think the time is long overdue for an examination by members of the House of

Commons, or by a joint committee, as has been suggested, of the over-all plan relating to the development of the capital of the nation. I believe there are a number of features about which there is not too great satisfaction at the moment, no matter what our regard may be for the individuals who serve as members of the federal district commission.
The truth is that while there is a Greber plan and while there has been a good deal of discussion of this subject, all with the best of intentions, like Topsy the capital has just "growed up". Land is bought here and land is bought there, without hon. members having any clear idea of the pattern being followed. A very worthy project, such as the construction of a new highway to the park area in the Gatineau, suddenly emerges without anyone being sure about what plan it relates to. There are other places where road facilities are not only not too good, but leave much to be desired.
I think it is desirable at this stage in the growth of Canada, particularly at a time when we have such evidence of rapidly increasing growth ahead, that hon. members who must assume the ultimate responsibility should consider this whole subject, and agree upon some over-all planning that would guide the federal district commission, guide the members of the government, and guide the House of Commons in future' parliaments.
One of the problems of course is the fact that there are municipalities with the ordinary municipal functions. I think it is quite clear that any measure of compulsion would not be acceptable either in the case of the city of Ottawa or in the case of the city of Hull. Success in carrying out these plans involves negotiation and co-operation between the federal district commission and the municipal councils concerned.
Undoubtedly that co-operation, and the planning of the federal district commission as well as that of the two municipalities, will be vastly facilitated by some clear understanding as to whether the Greber plan as such, or the Greber plan with modifications, or some completely new plan is to be accepted.
I do wish to refer to what may be regarded as only an incident, something to which the Prime Minister has already referred. He spoke about the entrance into Lady Grey drive from the new driveway on Sussex street. He mentioned that the turn that had been introduced there out of the new driveway into the Lady Grey drive was somewhat inconvenient. Mr. Chairman, it was more than that; it was extremely dangerous. Hon. members should not overlook something which may be symptomatic of a situation that should

be carefully checked. I strongly suspect that somebody laid out those plans on a paper with the cold concept of a route in front of him, without any thought of the speed of movement of traffic and what would happen when cars were suddenly forced to stop before making a sharp right-angle turn into that new driveway. If that alone had happened it would be different. What did happen, however, was that the angular entrance into the Lady Grey drive was closed. Now they have gone to all the expense of knocking away some of the new curb to put in a new roadway. I do not know how much has been wasted, but I know a great deal of money has been wasted on something that anybody with a reasonably good knowledge of planning of routes in these modern days would have anticipated.
It is not a case of wisdom after the event, because I know the Prime Minister realized the awkwardness of it the first time he went through there, and certainly the first time I went through there I found it difficult to understand how anybody could have created such a traffic hazard at this stage of the scientific development of highway construction.
In large measure the same situation exists at the other point the Prime Minister mentioned. A plan was drawn which on the ground provides ample width for cars as long as they are not moving. If they are moving, you suddenly find yourself in what is in effect a single passageway for one car after having had the full width of the passageway alone. I do not mention these to emphasize these two instances, each of which is going to cost a good deal of money to rectify. I mention them to suggest that it would be well in making future plans if steps were taken to ensure that routes of this sort will be designed on the assumption that automobiles do move and that even at 30 miles an hour, which is the declared speed limit, there is a momentum with tremendous effect on the general construction of routes of that kind.
I shall not add anything further to these remarks other than to say that all of us as members of this House of Commons, representative of the whole of Canada, do feel that the federal district commission has an important function to perform. We are all indebted to those ladies and gentlemen who at the present time and over the years past have devoted a great deal of time to this important public service. It is a part of the very natural instinct of a large and vigorous nation to make sure that the capital city is in all ways a city of which it can be proud, not only from the point of view of things that are done in the city or in the two cities
Supply-Privy Council that are joined in this plan, but also in the appearance that the cities will present to visitors from Canada and from ouside of Canada.

When I rose to ask the
Prime Minister a question or two I did so because I wondered whether certain questions might not be pertinent at this time. But the Prime Minister answered most of the questions I had in mind, and the point I had particularly in mind was about the appointment of a joint committee of this house and of the Senate to review the operations of the federal district commission.
I agree that the ladies and gentlemen who have been serving voluntarily on this commission deserve the best thanks of the House of Commons and indeed of the nation.
The Leader of the Opposition said, and the Prime Minister agreed, that there are many problems. There are a good many eyesores in this capital city which I hope one day will be removed. But what I was going to say is this: a few years ago I had the privilege of meeting some prominent people who had travelled all over the world. After dinner in the evening a discussion arose as to beautiful sites for capital cities. They placed three cities among several others as having the best sites, and they placed them in various order. One put Budapest first; another put Rio de Janeiro first; and another put Ottawa first. But always Ottawa appeared among the first three as one of the most beautiful sites for cities in the world.
A good deal of imagination has already been exercised by the federal district commission in laying out the attractive parklands around this city. The driveway is a lovely drive, enjoyed by all those who come to visit Ottawa. Beyond the city limits we have wonderful possibilities for a national park and for recreation, with numerous lakes and beautiful woodlands, rolling hills, and so on. I sincerely hope that when a parliamentary committee is established next session, it may not only review the operations of the federal district commission, but may give it encouragement to go ahead and give the city of Ottawa and the city of Hull encouragement also to remove some of the eyesores that now exist, to make their cities as beautiful as their surroundings. I know, as has already been said, whatever is done by the federal district commission with regard to beautification within the cities themselves will have to be done in co-operation with the municipal authorities.
It is a pity that when this city was established as the capital of Canada it was not made a federal district so that it could have

Supply-Privy Council been laid out appropriately under the direction and with the financial support of this parliament of Canada. However, that was not done. If I read the symptoms in Ottawa and Hull aright, the municipal authorities are going to hang on tenaciously to the rights that they have assumed or that have been granted to them under the provincial legislation that set them up. Therefore, we have to try to co-operate in every respect with them.
This parliament should not begrudge the money that will be required to make this capital city conform to the beauty of the surrounding countryside, the Gatineau hills and river, the beautiful countryside beyond its borders. I was glad to hear the Prime Minister say that the National Housing Act officials will safeguard the projected green belts around the cities of Ottawa and Hull.
I am looking forward to the parliamentary committee. I hoped to be on it if it were set up this year, and I certainly hope to be on it when it is set up next year.

I want to say only a few words, Mr. Chairman. I thank the Prime Minister for the excellent, lengthy survey he made of the federal district commission and its plans for the future. I also welcome, as others have, the announcement that surely next session we shall have a joint committee of the House of Commons and the Senate to study the operations of the national capital plan and the federal district commission in Ottawa and the adjoining areas. I have been asking for such a committee for some years, not that I thought the operations were not satisfactory, but I believed that hon. members should be better acquainted with the operations and also have a voice in the making of this national capital in the future.
There is one good thing about the survey report made by the Prime Minister. I think it is clear that the committee will not be bogged down with questions as to whether the federal government is taking over any of the rights of the municipality or the electors of this municipality. I believe that the electors of Ottawa have never had any great suspicion that the federal authorities wanted to take away their rights, but in any event the statement made by the Prime Minister this morning makes it clear that the primary concern of this committee, for the present at least, will not be to make of this area a federal district under the authority of the federal government.
One of the great difficulties that we have experienced with the plan is the fact that while there has been a master plan it has never received the approval of the municipal and provincial authorities, which authorities

are the essential ones in putting this project into effect. While it is true that this has had embarrassing effects on the federal district commission and the government, I want hon. members to realize that the fact that this plan has never been approved has made it difficult for the citizens at large who had lands or buildings within the areas mapped out on this plan.
It has not always been easy for the citizen of Ottawa to know what to do with his land. He does not know whether some day it may be expropriated or whether the Greber plan will be brought into effect. It is true that there were some bolder citizens who were willing to speculate and who went ahead knowing that it was legal in the sense that the municipal and provincial authorities would not stop them building. They went ahead while others with a greater sense of national responsibility did not do anything and then found their properties expropriated before they could take advantage of the improvements being made.
There is another feature which I have brought to the attention of the house before and which I have taken up privately with the Minister of Justice. I refer to the operation of the Expropriation Act. As the Prime Minister has said, the Expropriation Act is not used in the province of Quebec in connection with the acquisition of land, but it is used to a great extent in Ottawa and the province of Ontario. It is a very forceful weapon in the hands of those who must acquire land.
I must say that as a rule the citizens of Ottawa have not been satisfied with the results of land expropriations. I am speaking now of home owners. Those who have large buildings and possess the necessary resources can take care of themselves in the exchequer court, but the man who has only a small house finds himself in difficulties and must accept a price which in the opinion of many is too low.
I urge the government to consider doing something about the method of acquiring land for the federal district commission. The use of the Expropriation Act in its present form is really not called for. I have always contended that the Expropriation Act was not meant to be used to acquire land of this type or under the circumstances in which the federal district commission is acquiring land at the present time. I realize it is a long time since I went to law school but I have always looked upon the Expropriation Act as being a violation of civil rights. I submit that it should be used sparingly by the crown only in cases of great public interest, such as the acquisition of land for post

offices, wharves, national defence buildings and so on. It should not be used too readily. If it is to be used as in the present case all advantages should devolve upon the party whose property is being expropriated. On behalf of those hundreds of people whose properties have been expropriated in the district here and who are voicing discontent over this procedure, may I say that I hope the government will see that this parliamentary committee to be set up next session will make a complete study of the use of the Expropriation Act in acquiring land.
The time that elapses in the settlement of these cases is far too long. It may surprise some hon. members to know the time that elapses. These transactions are carried on by the federal district commission through the Department of Justice, and before the three parties involved can conclude an ordinary sale of land many months may elapse. I know of one case recently involving only $12,000 where the sale was not completed until after one year.
I welcome the fact that we are to have a committee to discuss the workings of the federal district commission and also, I hope, the operations of the Expropriation Act in connection with the national capital plan. I hope that hon. members will appreciate how much has been done in this area with the moneys which have been voted from year to year and that they will be kindly disposed in the future to approve expenditures so that this capital plan can be completed at a much faster rate than has been the case in the past.

Mr. Chairman, I do not rise to make a speech because I am sure we are all hoping against hope that we may finish earlier today than we did yesterday. Before I ask the question I have in mind may I pause to remark that it is interesting to contemplate the development of Ottawa as it has been described by the Prime Minister. I recall that it was only a few decades ago that an Englishman living in Toronto referred to Ottawa as an Arctic village. The Prime Minister referred to the green belt and I am not clear whether that is merely a picture on a map or whether it is still partially green. I was not clear from what the Prime Minister said whether steps are being taken to prevent further building on it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, most of what appears on the map as a green belt is still green. The only thing that the federal government can do at the present time to
Supply-Privy Council prevent the subdividing of that green belt for building purposes is to refuse to make any contributions under the National Housing Act toward the financing of such undertakings. Negotiations are going on in an effort to have the provinces and the municipalities give legal effect to this green belt.
But, as I mentioned, there is a problem. It is felt that there is the possibility of there being some unfairness to owners of land in the green belt if restrictions are placed upon those lands which do not apply outside of what is shown on the plan as the green belt. That is a matter about which municipal authorities and economists are not agreed.
Under the Quebec law the city simply homologates a line which constitutes a restriction upon owners of property enclosed within that homologated line and the owner gets no consideration because of restrictions being placed on his property. Some think that that is not fair. I think that this is something that should be looked at by this committee. Then the committee may come to the conclusion that some consideration should be given to providing compensation, and should then consider whether the compensation should come solely from the province and the municipality or whether the federal government should make some contribution to the compensation.

The Prime Minister used one phrase I should like to mention because it seemed to indicate the need for urgency. He spoke of the proper definition of the type of projects being carried out by the commission. I was struck with that phrase because it seemed to me that every month that was lost might create new difficulties.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: There is not always full agreement between the municipal authorities, the provincial authorities and the federal district commission as to what are the things the municipal authorities should do without any contribution and what are the things that are undertaken because this happens to be the capital and not merely a city of the present size. That has to be dealt with by negotiation. I think there has been very much progress made in the last four or five years in implementing the general outline of the plan. I think there is a genuine desire on the part of the municipal and provincial authorities and the federal district commission not to get as much from each other as they can, but to settle these problems on a basis that will appeal to most people as fair.

112. Departmental administration (including the former administration of employees' instalment purchase plan and employees' group insurance plans), $1,965,633.
Is the minister going to say anything?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I think there is no need of my making a statement. The estimates were considered in the estimates committee some two weeks ago and we had, if not a very extended, at least a fairly thorough consideration of the items that were placed before the committee. I should be glad to answer any questions that might be asked or make any observations that hon. members desire on particular points.

Mr. Chairman, as the minister has said, these estimates were before the committee on estimates. The hope was expressed there-and I hope I shall do nothing to belie it-that the time spent in this committee could thereby be lessened. I think we shall show that that is possible.
I wish, however, to make comments on one thing that came up before the committee,
EMr. St. Laurent.l
namely the operation of the treasury board. I should also like to make reference to a matter that came up at the time of the minister's speech in connection with his reduction of taxes. We had some talk at that time, and I could never quite disabuse my mind of the idea that the minister was teasing us a little. Members of the committee will remember that the only reason he was prepared to give for reducing the taxes was that he thought they were too high. That is a very good reason indeed, but we also thought he had probably done it to a certain extent to stimulate the economy. We could not interest the minister in that idea at all. He shied away from that.
It is with reference to that point that I wish to ask one or two questions. I think we are entitled to assume that the minister has given the matter a good deal of thought in the three months which have elapsed, and my questions will be based quite briefly on a C.P. report from London which appeared in the Globe and Mail of July 18. The report says this in part. This is a news story from Ottawa reported back from London:
The government now is veering round to the view that Canada's growth of population requires and justifies free spending on public projects even at the cost of increasing debts.
Later there is a further statement:
The policy "is obviously based on the view that any signs of repeated slackness next winter can be largely offset by public investment planned for its long-range usefulness in national development without too much regard to the budgetary situation of the moment."
I send this across to the minister so that he can have it for his convenience in answering. I would remind the minister, if he will allow me, that when we were discussing this in April I pointed out to him that deficit financing was like drink. It is apt to get hold of you and apt to become very attractive. It is for this reason that I am putting this report before the minister and hoping that he may say something about it.
Of course, if the minister's answer is that his views are along this line and that we are going to follow what was regarded as the Keynesian view that we can spend our way through, then the next thing I am going to discuss might seem to be irrelevant because it is the old topic of economy. I do not believe the minister is one who has economy out of his mind, and certainly I have not.
So for a few moments I propose to talk about the treasury board, which is really our front-line trench, one might say, in resisting the onslaught of extravagance. I want to confine myself to non-defence expenditure because, of course, in the first place, defence expenditures are almost untouchable

and, secondly, one gets into mysteries that those of us who are not familiar with up-to-date war are not very well versed in.
I should like to begin these remarks by referring to a speech made by the minister's predecessor in 1950 and reported on page 1214 of Hansard. I have always remembered what Mr. Abbott said at that time. Whilst no one wants to hold him to the predictions he mentioned, because no one could foresee the glad years we have had since, nevertheless this is what he said. I would suggest to the committee that what has happened since shows that economy is not too much with us and that a good deal of effort is still necessary in that direction. This is what Mr. Abbott said:
Our efforts to hold expenditures ... I have described .	.	. we must cope somehow with a
continuing level oi expenditure of $2,400 million, ... I doubt if the public or this House of Commons will really wish government services or activities to be reduced in years of prosperity to the degree necessary to get our expenditures much below this level of $2,400 million.
That is five years ago. I am sure the minister will share with me the irony of that statement because our non-defence expenditures for the present year are going to be about $2,920 million against $1,957 million non-defence expenditures in 1950. In other words, they will have gone up in those five years about $965 million. I should be quick to point out that a large part of that amount is for old age security, something like $367 million. That would bring it down to somewhere near a $600 million increase in the five years. Again one must immediately draw attention to some other amounts. For instance, at that time the province of Ontario was not receiving money under the dominion-provincial agreement. There are other substantial amounts too. But I wish to draw attention to just three or four of the ordinary amounts in departments which have not experienced any revolutionary change in that time. Public works is up $61 million; transport is up $35 million; national revenue only $8 million; external affairs, $33 million. That is becoming more expensive. Citizenship and immigration is up $91 million. I am not going to take the time of the committee to delve further into that matter. I submit that I have made a prima facie case that we need to watch the bawbees, that we need to economize as much as we can.
It is for that reason that I was interested, when we were before the estimates committee, to get a close-up of the treasury board. Treasury board has always been a rather mythical organization to me up until this time. I have heard about the terrors that face people that go before the treasury board.
Supply-Finance
I was therefore interested to come to be a little bit more familiar with this organization. I was a little bit disappointed. I did not feel that it was quite as terrifying an organization as I would have liked it to be. It consisted of a group of ministers, mostly

if I may say this with respect-rather junior ministers. To my surprise I found that the comptroller of the treasury does not sit on the board. But it was explained to me that he is only concerned with seeing that the money is properly spent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No. It was explained to you that the treasury board was a committee of the cabinet.

Yes. I think I understood that. Then in addition to the ministers mentioned there are present, when each department is reviewed, several senior officials of the Department of Finance, and of course senior officials of the department concerned. The method of operation is naturally one that one would expect. The preparation of the estimates is done by the department concerned. Then the treasury board examines these estimates and each department is discussed by the treasury board. When examining anything, one is always anxious to have evidence from outside and from people who may seem to be impartial. I therefore read to the committee a statement emanating from the Winnipeg Free Press and which indeed I had brought to the attention of this house once before. I read it again:
Careful study of the federal civil service indicated that the cause of the hitherto uncontrollable growth was simple. Whenever there was a need for expansion, the departments expanded. They did not search within themselves for surplus personnel and meet the need for expansion by making better use of their existing staff. They invariably added to it.
Let me digress for a moment to say that that procedure seems to me to be extremely undesirable on two grounds. First of all, it is undesirable in automatically adding to the civil service and, second, in not making sure that the good jobs that are going are available primarily to people who are already in the civil service. I continue the quotation:
To illustrate: If a bridge is built across the St. Lawrence, there would have to be a customs house at the Canadian end of it, staffed by customs and immigration officers. The opening of the bridge would greatly reduce the number of people entering the country by ferries but instead of transferring them from the ferry ports to the bridge, the tendency would be to add to the payroll by appointing additional staff at the bridge.
What I am quoting comes from a staff writer of the Winnipeg Free Press. I therefore think I can assume that it is not prejudiced against the government. This item and other things put us on inquiry and we

Supply-Finance
were interested to find in the committee where the responsibility lay. We asked the Minister of Finance about this matter. This was the question asked of the minister: when we find this happening according to the Winnipeg Free Press, we must not blame the customs department but we must blame the treasury board. To this the minister replied, "No; blame the Minister of Finance". That does not really help because, however generous the minister may be, it does not solve the problem.
We went on to ask the minister whether -as I most certainly had understood-the fact was that the finance department exercised supervision over other departments. I want to point out that representatives of the senior officials of the finance department do go and confer with the representatives of the department in question. But when the minister was asked whether there was supervision over other departments the answer was this:
We are only discussing my own department. X do not tnink there is need for it-
That is for outside supervision.
-in that department.
Then further he was questioned as to the other departments or any other departments and what might be the need for investigation, and his answer was this:
You would not expect me to say that any other department ought to be investigated.
That came to me in a way as a surprise because I thought that somebody must be responsible and I assumed that it was the Department of Finance. But apparently the real answer is that in each department- subject to the scrutiny of certain officials of the finance department-the minister and his staff allow his conscience to be their guide. When the minister had it pointed out to him that certain departments-notably post office and the film board, I think-had outside investigation and he was asked under what circumstances was it found that there was investigation in this case, the answer by the minister was this:
You would have to ask the departments concerned.
My query about that matter is this. I entirely failed to find what seemed to me to be the real responsibility. I think the minister would say that I am overlooking the senior officials-and very good officials they are-who go to department A, department B and department C and discuss the situation. But I cannot imagine a senior official, however good he is, being able, with a deputy minister,-and deputy ministers are rather formidable people-to go into a department and not merely do a little bit
[Mr. Macdonnell.l
of chiselling here and a little bit of chiselling there but discuss the whole question of reorganization as an outside visitor might do. I am going to discuss that outside inspection for a moment or two. The minister's final comment on that matter was this:
Perhaps we could agree on the general proposition that these business firms (efficiency firms) are useful in their own field.
I was disappointed by that answer because it seemed to me to imply that there was one standard of efficiency in the business world and an entirely different standard in the government, which would be a kind of mystery to anyone coming from the outside. I am just using the words uttered by the minister and from them drawing what inferences I can.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: If you want me to use the word "misleading", I can use it right here.

I am using the minister's words and he can correct my inferences if they are wrong. The implications seemed to me to be those which I have suggested. I will read the words again:
Perhaps we could agree on the general proposition that these business firms (efficiency firms) are useful in their own field.
I want to spend a moment or two on the question of these efficiency firms. We asked why they were brought into the post office and the minister's answer was that we would have to ask the department concerned. I want to read a part of the report of the efficiency firm, Woods, Gordon and company. With regard to the operations branch of the Post Office Department the report has this to say:
The work of the operations branch has over the years increased to the point where the staff at all levels are overloaded with a multitude of routine problems and correspondence. No one has had the time to develop policies which can be applied on an over-all basis.
Later the report says:
The branch is operating under a severe handicap as there are no standards established to measure the relative efficiency of a given method of operation. The lack of such standards is particularly felt when requests are received for additions to staff or accommodation.
I can well believe that. I repeat what I said a moment ago, that as between some outside independent persons coming in, as was done in the case of the post office, outside people with no strings on them, as between an independent and presumably efficient inspection of that kind and that which would be conducted by even the very best civil servants, there is, I submit, a world of difference. In the one case you have a person who is absolutely at arm's length, and in the other case I submit you have not to the same extent.

I remember being told that when Winston Churchill as a young man became first lord of the admiralty he summoned all the senior members of the staff and asked them what they were doing. When they got to the end of the story he then asked them a question they had never been asked before. He said, "Why?" In other words, what he was doing was to query the organization right from the foundation up. Nothing was sacred, nothing was untouchable, everything had to be submitted to scrutiny and justify itself or it would be changed.
Personally I have never been a civil servant, but I find it impossible to believe that a civil servant could go into the department of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, let us say, and tell him that there was some basic reorganization that was needed in his department. Such a man ought to have the V.C. I just cannot see it happening, and that is why I come back again-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: It does not need reorganization.

There you are. That is the real spirit. It does not need it. But what I would say to the senior member for Halifax is that in the business world, where there are, I think, able people, people who have been trained to their jobs, it is recognized that it is a good thing to get a fresh outside mind to come in and see what they are doing. I want to stress again the Minister of Finance's own words-"You would not expect me to say that any other department ought to be investigated". I admit it would be a difficult thing to do, but at the present time the only person who can say that a department should be investigated is the minister concerned himself, and I submit that is utterly and absolutely unsound.
If there is a skeleton in the cupboard, if the minister is conscious that there are things that are not right, unless the minister is a very unusual person both in character and ability he is not going to bring in strangers and give them full scope to see what is going on. He is going to hide it and, as I say, unless he is a very unusual man he will not regard the hiding as anything improper. He will be quite sure that he is going to clear it up himself next month or at the most in two months. He will not be conscious he is doing anything wrong. He will not feel in the least that he is doing anything wrong. Again I say it would only be a man of unusual character and ability who would do that.
I submit that on the basis of what I have said, and it all comes out of this memorandum, there is nothing to indicate that there is a really searching inquiry going on now. There is nothing I could see in what we
Supply-Finance
heard, and I repeat, why should that be true only in government business? After all, government operation in a way is a piece of cake because the government can fix its own income. They are not subject to the hard law of the market where a company only nas the income which it earns. If the government has not got enough income they can take more out of our pockets. Therefore there is a great danger that money does not mean quite the same to them as it does to somebody who is handling a business which, if it does not succeed, goes broke with the result that the person in charge probably loses his job and comes to a sad end.
The answer may very well be made that you are only talking about ministers and ministers may not be trained in administration. As a matter of fact, a good many of them are not. Their talents often lie in other and very useful directions, directions which bring them to this house, directions which enable the government to stay in office but which may not necessarily have any very close connection with administration. Take the civil servants. My answer is that if the civil servants are to be regarded as the second line of defence-in some ways they are really the first line of defence-then I would like someone to show me a good civil servant, a top-ranking civil servant, and I will venture to say I can persuade him it would be a very good thing for him to have some able outside person come in and discuss with him his operations.
Take, for example, the Department of National Defence, and I have mentioned this in the house before. When the minister's predecessor was here I never could get rid of the idea that he felt by working like a demon, working ten times as hard as anyone else, he was going to be able to get the thing going all right.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: So he did.

In my opinion that was always the greatest mistake. If the minister is assuming, without more knowledge than I think he can possibly have of the Department of National Defence, that everything is all right, he will have to allow me to say that I regard other opinions of his as of more value than that one. At any rate, there you have a department with tens of thousands of civilian employees. When the question was raised as to what had been done to scrutinize the organization the minister just said, as far as I can remember, that they had a job and they were doing it, and certainly if hard work and application were the key he had it.

Supply-Finance
I have never been able to understand why there was an adamant unwillingness on the part of the government to avail themselves of outside assistance. When this matter was brought up by our party and discussed earlier in the year the government took no part in the debate whatever. They did not think it was even necessary to answer what was said. I suggest that prima facie the course I am suggesting is reasonable for three reasons.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I suppose you realize you are out of order. We had a vote on this subject once.

Perhaps the chairman will tell me if I am. I am nearly through. These are the three reasons: 1. With a business of nearly $5 billion, it stands to reason that even a little additional efficiency will pay off in a big way. 2. In the United States this plan has been adopted with beneficial results.
3.	In two of our own departments it has been done and it was found that it was worth-while.
As a result of the experience I had in the committee, if the government is not ready to bring in outside assistance which, incidentally,
1	would hope would offer comments on the present organization and comments as to the relationship of the treasury board with the departments, then I suggest to the government that they should have a very good look at the treasury board itself because so far as I was able to discern as a result of the evidence given to us there is at the present time no real responsibility. You cannot find where the real responsibility is, and I cannot imagine a worse criticism that could be made of any organization than that.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to discuss a matter that has been brought to my personal attention by several municipalities in British Columbia. I understand municipalities in Ontario and western Canada generally are anxious to have this matter brought before the minister. I refer to the reopening of the Municipal Improvements Assistance Act. This act is still on the statute books but has been inoperative for 14 or 15 years.
Its history is a very good one. When it did operate some of the municipalities were in a pretty shaky condition, but under that measure they were able to borrow money at
2	per cent for self-liquidating projects. Without a single exception all the principal and all the interest was paid back on every loan. Therefore it is hard to understand why the department is reluctant to continue this excellent service to municipalities.
As hon. members know, British Columbia has almost doubled its population in the last

ten years. The municipalities are facing a difficult situation, inasmuch as the area originally incorporated as a city has not increased, and there is a heavy burden placed on the handful of land owners who have to bear the higher costs of education and operation of the city in general. All the increase in population is not necessarily in the established towns. I visited recently outside of Vancouver where a totally new area is being developed. Obviously they have no credit, because they are not an established community. The residents are mostly returned men. They need public improvements such as sewers and roads, and all the facilities required by a new town. However, with no' credit and with no established history as a city they find it difficult to borrow money.
I feel this fund should be reopened to-serve communities of that kind, so that they could borrow money at 2 per cent when,, otherwise, they have to go on the market and, in view of their inability to offer adequate security, they have to pay 5 or 6 per cent.
The sum available under the act today is $30 million, and that amount is frozen. I suggest that immediately it be increased to $100 million, and the fund reopened. About half the cities in British Columbia would be delighted to borrow some of this money. I know some of them need new waterworks. They are carrying on with obsolete piping systems and obsolete dams, but they just do not have the money to make these improvements. One town I have in mind would like to borrow $150,000, but they are afraid to go on the open market because they are already up to their necks in debt because of the building of hospitals and the like.
Therefore I would ask the minister to study the provisions of the act so that he may learn the good accomplished under it while it operated. He would find out about the public works it had helped to build, and the excellent history of payments made by those who borrowed. Many municipalities in British Columbia have requested that the benefits of this act be made available to them. I do not think the minister has had time to find out exactly how it operated, or why the fund has been frozen. However, I appeal to him on behalf of all these towns to give consideration to increasing the sum available from $30 million to $100 million at once, and again allowing municipalities to borrow at the rate of 2 per cent for self-liquidating works.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to approach this whole matter of the Department of Finance in this way: I feel the only time we have during the year to discuss effectively the minister's budget speech is on the occasion of the appearance before the

committee of supply of the estimates for the Department of Finance. I am not sure that I am putting the correct interpretation on the situation but I believe I am.
We know that in the United States they listen to a speech every year known as the "state of the nation" speech. In Canada I believe the budget speech is the one delivered by the government to indicate the state of the nation. Consequently when we consider the budget speech and the estimates of the Department of Finance we are considering the state of the nation.
My first observations will be of a negative character, but they will set out exactly the kind of problems which will be confronting the dominion-provincial conference in October. And those problems will have to be solved.
May I approach the minister's estimates with this general point of view: I would like to congratulate the minister upon the work he has done already in his department, and I would say for the record, so that people out in the country who read may learn, that this is the minister's first year, and that he is not responsible for the unhappy conditions which have developed in Canada but which he, and men like him who will succeed him, must solve, or see the Canadian nation probably fall apart. As I said, I should like to congratulate him upon the way he has taken hold of the general situation. What I shall say is not in any sense by way of criticism of the minister, but simply a matter of reviewing the problems and of seeing whether or not we can find some ideas that might solve those problems, ideas which up to the present time we have not put into operation or implemented.
I was impressed, as I am sure were other hon. members, by the speech delivered by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre on May 10. It was a thoughtful speech, and was the first of its kind I had heard given in the house. It greatly impressed me. He said, in effect, that the parliament of Canada is losing its prestige because, whereas parliament should lead the nation and should lay down policy for the provinces to follow, what is actually happening is that the provinces, after seeing the dominion government in operation for the number of years it has been in office, have given up all hope of solving their problems through the federal government, and are now seeking more and more to hold provincial conferences of the kind they held when the federal government was first established.
I thought the hon. member's speech was well developed, and that there was good sound reasoning in it. If there is truth, if there
Supply-Finance
is validity in the general position taken by the hon. member, I am sure the minister will agree with me that the situation constitutes a real challenge to Canada. It is a challenge to the finance department. Just to indicate how serious the situation could be the provincial representatives who will meet in these conferences will have much less opportunity of devising new ways and means than there would be in the minister's department, in the cabinet or in a caucus of the Liberal party. Now, certain reasons will apply. In the first place, when the provincial representatives meet they will not all be alike politically in their thinking, or economically in their thinking. You can imagine the difficulty of seeing eye to eye that will develop between British Columbia and Ontario or Alberta and Nova Scotia or New Brunswick just because we have Social Credit thinking in one province and we have strictly Conservative thinking in another, whatever that means. I have never been able quite to figure out what Conservatives do stand for, but that is a sufficient indication of the difficulty.
We know what we stand for.

The way is open for you to tell. I do not hesitate to tell what we stand for, but I have never heard Conservatives say what they stand for. I am merely illustrating Ihe point that there will be a tendency for a clash between those who meet in provincial conferences.
Again, the average provincial expert is not a federal expert. A man who has spent his life working on provincial problems has not had the opportunity to think federally. Consequently, for a group of provincial men to grapple with the problems of high finance which have to be grappled with by the minister and his department is just a very difficult thing, perhaps a high improbability.
There will also be a clash of sectional interests among members of the provincial conference. For example, the interests of Ontario or Quebec are certainly not the interests of Prince Edward Island, and they are not the interests of Saskatchewan. There will be a clash of sectional interests, and then there will be a shortage of time and there will be a lack of finance to employ the best experts. Consequently, I see, or I think I see-I do not want to be too gloomy; I want to face facts as they are-a real danger implicit in the development of more and more provincial conferences with the object of solving the problems of Canada taking precedence over the dominion government. Therefore, I do not see very much hope ultimately from the provincial conferences.
I am sure the minister saw the report of Premier Smallwood's statement to the effect

Supply-Finance
that he would be leading a secession move. I know the Prime Minister more or less endeavoured to gloss this over in the house, to laugh it off; but I do not think the report which we find in the Ottawa Journal justifies one in treating lightly what this man said. In the Ottawa Journal of June 21, 1955, we find this statement:
Newfoundland may quit Canada, premier's threat.
St. Andrews-by-the-Sea, N.B., June 21-(BUP) -
Premier Joseph Smallwood threatened last night to lead Newfoundland out of confederation with Canada unless the federal government stopped discriminating against the four Atlantic provinces, including his own.
Smallwood issued his blunt notice at the annual meeting of the Atlantic association of broadcasters.
His threat of quitting Canada was given added weight by the presence of premier Henry Hicks, of Nova Scotia, a Liberal, and premier Hugh John Flemming, of New Brunswick, a Conservative. Flemming introduced Smallwood in glowing terms and Hicks praised him for "talking the way we should in the Atlantic provinces".
This is what is reported further:
Economy Lopsided
"This may not be good Liberalism, nor good politics", the aggressive premier of Canada's youngest province Said. "But Canada is not just four provinces, Quebec, Ontario, British Columbia and Alberta. It is 10 provinces."
"The Canadian economy is becoming lopsided. The federal government will spend billions of dollars in war contracts in Ontario and Quebec. There is nothing wrong in those provinces becoming industrial giants", Smallwood said. "But if they are to show statesmanship they should make every province economically strong."
"It is not good for Canada to leave these Atlantic provinces to their own resources," he said.
His thinly-veiled threat:
"Before we become second-class citizens of Canada, we will show the other maritime provinces how to get out of confederation." There was a storm of applause from the audience.
I am not just sure that I have the completion of the statement, but I believe this is the completion of the press report. In any case, it is sufficient and I think I shall leave it at that. There is enough warning in it, I would say, to make anyone in Canada very serious.
It must be quite obvious to anyone who stops and thinks a little that when any province came into the Dominion of Canada there was implicit in the contract the ideal that that province would be able to share on equal terms all the good things that all the provinces can produce. If that is the case, and I see no way of explaining the proposition away, then undoubtedly there is a very heavy responsibility resting upon the minister and his department to see to it that every province in this dominion is able to share adequately in the good things that Canada can produce. Up to the present time that happy condition has never been brought about by any government that has held
[Mr. Blackmore.l
power in Ottawa. I maintain there is no reason why it should not be brought about. Evidently Premier Smallwood feels about the same way. In other words, the dominion government has utterly failed in the major responsibility of seeing that every province in this dominion shares equally in the good things this dominion can produce.
The question is, what are we going to do about it? My general position, Mr. Chairman, is this. We can keep on carrying on in this parliament for a hundred years, using the same ideas which we have employed up to the present time in managing this country, and never change the situation at all. Now, what can be done about it?
The other day in another connection I said this: If we could create money, as was done under the Finance Act of 1914, if we could create money in Ottawa and issue that money to Nova Scotia, to Prince Edward Island or to any other of the maritime provinces, if we could do that, we would enable those provinces to buy any goods available for sale in the Dominion of Canada.
I will ask anyone in the committee and anyone in the country whether that is not true? If we undertake to tax money from the more fortunate provinces of Quebec, Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia and give that money to the maritimes, obviously we are being unfair to those provinces from which we tax the money. But if we can create the money as was done, remember, under the Finance Act of 1914-to anyone who wants to talk about funny money I say, just fix your eyes on the Finance Act of 1914 and hold your peace until you see your way through. If we can create money as they did under that Finance Act and put that money into the hands of the people, what will happen? They will be able to enjoy the good things that the other provinces produce and will provide markets for the other provinces, which is exactly what we all want, and at the same time the process will cost no one a dollar.
I do not feel that it would be becoming for me to go on with this problem too far before I gave a hint of what might form the solution. Let it be borne in mind that we are in an age of superabundance. Surely everybody knows that. Not only do we have the production which we have been able to bring into being in each of the various provinces of Canada, not only do we have that and all that we can bring into being in the future by similar means, but we are now entering into whole new fields of productive capacity, as is witnessed by a report in the Ottawa Journal of June 11 stating that the atom is opening the way to synthetic foods.

Every hon. member has heard about the culture of algae and of the simply astounding things that are possible with respect to producing through algae culture every kind of food for human beings. If we brought into Canada the use of the atom to produce synthetic foods and the use of algae to produce new foods, can anyone conceivably see any reason why the people of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Newfoundland or of any other province should be in the slightest degree in need? If they continue in need, then it is somebody's fault and the only one whose fault it could possibly be is the Minister of Finance, except in so far as he might be bound by a lack of comprehension on the part of those who are about him. I suggest that the solution which I have offered thus far constitutes a way around the difficulty I have mentioned and that without that solution there is no way around. Let anyone who wishes to answer what I have to say tell where there is a way around.
There are some eleven serious problems facing Canada. The first is the centralization of industry and population and consequent control in Canada. In the last redistribution Saskatchewan lost members; other provinces lost members. Where did those members go but into Ontario and Quebec? What does that mean? That means that the political control of the destinies of Canada to the extent that members went from the western and eastern provinces into Ontario and Quebec was further centralized in Ontario and Quebec. Under those circumstances how can we pretend that we have in Canada a growing democracy?
