What is the solution? Obviously it is the decentralization of industry. How can industry be decentralized? I am thinking at the present moment of a woollen mill which was established in Magrath in my constituency. We thought we had everything necessary to set up and run a good woollen mill, but we could not manufacture any goods to speak of that could not be manufactured in Ontario and Quebec and sent out there to undersell our goods and put our mill right out of business. Under circumstances like that, tell me how we can ever decentralize the business of textile manufacturing and establish any considerable amount of it in Alberta, Saskatchewan, Nova Scotia or Newfoundland.
It is one thing to talk about decentralizing industry; it is another thing to do it. Saskatchewan under its government has made noble efforts to establish industry, but they have come into collision with the same forces. The great sums of money which they have expended in establishing these industries,
Supply-Finance
absolutely soundly expended, have been lost. It has been shown once more that it is going to be impossible in this country-unless something is done-to decentralize industry in any real sense of the term.
How are we going to get around the difficulty? I maintain that if it is possible to use money in such a way as to subsidize the price of woollen goods or textiles manufactured in southern Alberta so that they may compete successfully with those produced in Ontario and Quebec, then by that means we can enable industries to develop in Alberta or Saskatchewan. By that means we can enable industry to develop in the four maritime provinces thereby providing in them employment and increasing population and the use of their resources.
If there is any other way in which it can be done, let anyone who thinks he knows that way rise in this committee and tell us. If there is any reason why it cannot be done by that means, let anyone rise and tell us why. That is the first problem. That is the problem that Mr. Smallwood pointed his finger at. Unless we can get industry developed in the other provinces we can never be anything but hewers of wood and drawers of water in the eight provinces of Canada; hewers of wood and drawers of water for Ontario and Quebec, although those two provinces may not want it to be that way at all.
Another problem is the inadequate use of resources, which ties right in to what I have just said about the development of industry. If we cannot have woollen mills in southern Alberta we cannot use our sheep and our pastures to the advantage to which we could use them if we could manufacture our own textiles in southern Alberta. Therefore all those resources are lying idle, and so with the great resources of the other less favoured provinces. Their resources are lying idle while the resources of the two central provinces are being used in large measure. Obviously that is not a sound state of affairs in a country like Canada and in a world which requires so much production. What are we going to do about it? I maintain that there is a chance of solving it by using a monetary technique and I maintain that there is no chance of solving it by any other means.
The third important problem is the inadequacy of provincial control over credit. When the Social Credit government went in in Alberta-I am using this as an illustration- we found the bankers presiding at their desks like lords over domains. If a man came in to seek a loan he almost had to get to his knees or lower down and plead for it. If

Supply-Finance
Alberta had no means whereby she could bring pressure to bear on the banks to lend money to men who wished to produce, how could Alberta possibly have any real control over the prosperity of her people? When loans were granted Alberta borrowers had to pay 8 per cent. The ordinary farmer who needed to borrow money to produce a crop had to pay 8 per cent, and even at that he had his note discounted. The hon. member for Peace River was one of the members of the Social Credit government who faced the problem in Alberta. It is quite obvious that when Alberta began we had no effective control at all over our credit in that province. Would anyone pretend that a state of affairs like that was sound, or that a province had any chance whatever of giving good government while conditions like that prevailed?
I am going to tell you something about the maritimes. When the maritimes were independent, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick had their own banks. People could go into those banks and borrow money to set up any kind of industry which the banks might consider a sound proposition. After they entered confederation, it was not long before large banks such as the Royal Bank of Canada, the Bank of Montreal and other banks in Ontario and Quebec acquired a controlling interest in the banks in the maritimes and were able thereby to bring to Toronto and Montreal the control of lending in the maritimes. There were even cases where industries whose products were competing with corresponding industries in Ontario and Quebec were cut off from credit and closed up. As long as a condition like that continues, Nova Scotia, Newfoundland, or any other province similarly situated can only pretend to be able to control its own household.
What did we do in Alberta? First of all we set up a treasury branch. I am using this to illustrate what I mean by provincial control of credit. Fortunately, according to our constitution the Alberta government had a right to loan money from the provincial treasury. I think there were only two provinces that had that right. The hon. member for Peace River, faced with the problem, conceived the idea of setting up a branch of the treasury in a given place to allow people to come in and borrow money.
He saw that the day would come when such treasury branches would be established all over the province, and those treasury branches would lend money to men who were worthy of credit at 5 per cent interest. Imagine the difference to the economy of Alberta when every dollar borrowed by Albertans could be borrowed at 5 per cent, as contrasted with 8 per cent from the banks.
[Mr. Blackmore.l
Those who talk about Alberta's prosperity depending on her discovery of oil completely overlook that little matter, which is a very big matter.
As soon as the treasury branches got into operation, the banks realized that they were losing money, and I know of bankers who buttonholed in the street men whom they had previously refused, telling them they could borrow money now and at lower rates. The result was that the treasury branches enabled Alberta to bring down the bank rate and bring down the requirements for borrowing money. So it was not really necessary to establish treasury branches all over the province in order for Alberta to exercise control over her credit. If we could let Nova Scotia or any other province that has had difficulties of the same kind have treasury branches, they could do something similar to what Alberta did, with tremendous advantage to the economy.
We went further than that, and this is just another illustration. When our Social Credit government assumed office in Alberta, all the money our municipalities were borrowing in order to put in waterworks and other facilities had to be borrowed, almost all of it, in the open market and that generally meant New York. They paid a high rate of interest, 6 or 7 per cent. You know what Alberta is doing now? As a result of the blessings we have had through wisely managing our oil, we have been able to save a considerable amount of money, some hundreds of millions. We have used that money to lend to the municipalities, to electrification organizations and to other organizations at 2 and 3 per cent, thereby saving a tremendous amount of money to all those municipalities. We have been lending the money on much longer terms and on such terms that all the interest on the money that used to go to New York stays home in the province of Alberta.
The hon. member for Peace River reminds me that that sort of thing prevents competition in the open market. With our provincial debt, when Social Credit went in our over-all rate was 4 9 per cent. Now it is 2 78 per cent.
I have said enough to indicate what I mean by a province controlling its credit. If any province cannot control credit within its boundaries, it can hardly control anything with respect to its economy. Nothing has been done throughout the years by any minister of finance of Canada to remedy that situation. Are we going to let that state of affairs continue, or are we going to do something about it?
Here is another important problem. There is inadequacy of provincial control over markets. I referred to that in connection with

a local textile mill in Alberta. If a province establishing an industry within its boundaries is to be denied access to the markets of that province, certainly it is denied everything that can make the industry succeed.
That is one of the serious mishaps that-occurred to the provinces when they entered confederation. Before Nova Scotia and New Brunswick entered confederation they were able to have their markets themselves. Now their markets belong to Ontario and Quebec. That state of affairs simply cannot continue.
I hope the minister sees that. If we are ever going to have a sound, economically healthy and happy Canada with the population all over the country using our resources and benefiting by them, some sort of device must be worked out whereby any given province can at least have some kind of control over its own markets.
People will ask, "How are you going to accomplish that?" You do not need to set up tariff barriers. All you have to do is subsidize the goods produced in the province sufficiently so that similar goods coming in from Ontario and Quebec will not be able to undersell them. You do not have to set up tariffs. Will anybody tell me that device would not work, if you had the money? Will anyone tell me that device could not be applied with almost infinite benefit to the maritime provinces, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, if we had the money?
Another problem we face is this. It has been emphasized-and I know the minister is worried about this-by what has happened in Canada since 1946. The minister knows that in 1946 the dominion government permitted the steel companies of Canada to raise the price of steel by $5. Immediately the steel workers struck, and they continued on strike for 82 days until finally they were granted a share of the money that was involved in that increase. That increase of $5 a ton raised the price of goods all over Canada, directly and indirectly, to the terribly high prices they are at now, and cut the value of the Canadian dollar from $1 to about 53 cents. Because labouring men all over struck for higher wages, the cost of production of everything again went up, and so we are where we are now.
The provinces suffered by that rise in prices. The loss which Alberta and other, provinces- in fact every province-sustained by reason of that rise in price because of that move in connection with steel only-not because too much money was put into circulation-is almost beyond the power to compute. And the provinces could do nothing at all about it.
As to the power in Canada that might have done something about it, what did they do?
Supply-Finance
What did the finance minister of those days do? He did just completely nothing. The provinces were left all unprotected against that terrible rise in prices. Now what do we find? We find another rise in steel prices, if you please, down in the United States which will result before very long in another rise in steel prices in Canada, comparable no doubt with the $5 increase in 1946. And what do you suppose that price rise will do to the value of the dollar? If it does not cut the value of the Canadian dollar in two again I shall be greatly surprised.
What is the minister thinking of doing about the matter? Are we to turn the provinces over to the spoilers again so that billions and billions of dollars can be literally stolen again from the people of the various provinces by the men who are in a position to produce and sell goods? That is what I mean by inadequacy of dominion control over prices in Canada.
Some people may say, "Do you propose slapping on iron-clad controls?" My reply is, "No, I do not propose anything nonsensical like that." Social Credit does not favour iron-clad controls. Social Credit favours persuasive means through a monetary technique similar in principle to the one I have indicated, giving a province control over its own credit. In 1935 a law might have been passed forbidding interest rates above 5 per cent. That law would be a control, but it would not have been anything like as effective. That procedure would not have got us very far. What did Alberta do? By competition she brought the interest rates down in a way that laws and controls never could have done. There are devices of that sort that can be used. All we have to do is to explore them if we can get the money. Now can we get the money?
The important thing to bear in mind is that money is only a ticket for goods. You cannot have any money on a desert. The more goods you have in a country the more money you can have, for the real backing of money is goods. We can produce goods to further abundance in Canada. The minister expects $26J- billion this year in Canada, does he not, and probably much more than that. I am positive we can easily double that amount if we set about doing it. If there were enough markets and sufficient demand in Canada, we could probably double that $26 billion. If we can produce the goods, why can we not have the money? That is a point which needs careful consideration.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
I am sorry to be compelled to interrupt the hon. member, but it is my duty to inform him that his 40 minutes' time has expired.

Supply-Finance
Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I shall continue this discussion after a while, when I have an opportunity.

Mr. Chairman, my reason for entering this debate at this time is the fact that a few days ago I had a communication from an important part of our potato industry expressing concern over the forecast surplus production of potatoes in the United States to the extent of an estimated 50 million bushels.
Most of my remarks will concern the potato industry in my own province, but I should like to point out that the problem of which I speak is of concern to the industry right across Canada. Representatives of that industry across Canada met and expressed their concern to the tariff board at a hearing requested by the minister. I do not think 1 can introduce my subject in any better way than by reading a few excerpts from the letter or order which the minister gave to the tariff board at that time. I quote:
I have received numerous representations to the effect that there has been a significant increase in imports of potatoes in recent years, and that this has caused serious concern among Canadian potato producers.
In these representations it has been urged that the customs duty on potatoes be increased and that tne period to which the seasonal duty applies be extended.
That ends the quotation for the time being. I might note that the letter then gives the tariff scale, which indicates that except for the period between the middle of June and the end of July there is no tariff at all on United States potatoes coming into Canada. I should explain that United States potatoes were not indicated as such, but United States potatoes are what we are concerned with. They are what is referred to in the letter as getting favoured nation tariff treatment.
The minister asked the board for the most complete information that can be obtained regarding production, consumption, marketing, imports and exports of potatoes, and the effects on Canadian producers and consumers of the operation of the Canadian tariff relative to potatoes in their natural state. I might say that the tariff scale was arranged, I believe, about 16 years ago. At that time I think perhaps it did make good sense. W. J. Callaghan, a former tariff commissioner, a native islander who grew up not far from my own home, said this in part in presenting the brief of Prince Edward Island to that board:
In former years we exported substantial quantities of table stock to the United States and imported supplies from that country only when fresh supplies were not readily available in our own country, or in the occasional year when our domestic crop was below normal.
[The Deputy Chairman.]
But I might say that the trend has changed. In recent years United States imports have reached alarming proportions. After the cessation of United States guaranteed prices-I think it was in 1951-the United States growers apparently found there was a ready market available close to home, so they poured their spuds into our country. Now they ship in more than we ship to them. In the last three years, for example, we have shipped 7 million bushels to the United States and they have shipped 9 million bushels into Canada.
As I have indicated previously, when the present tariff structure was arranged apparently it made sense. The potato movement between this country and the United States was a one-way movement for the most part, certainly so far as the late crop was concerned. But that is true no longer. By the way, this tariff which is now in effect for six weeks in the summer is designed to protect the very early growers in Canada, and I believe it applies to those in southern Ontario and southern British Columbia. With that I have no quarrel at all. I am just pointing out that fact. I should emphasize again that those people ship their potatoes into Canada without any duty at all except for the period I mentioned. I might explain that we pay 37 i cents on our quota, which is 21 million bushels of seed potatoes and 1 million bushels of table stock, and 75 cents per hundredweight on anything over that amount.
It is interesting to note that the United States quota of one million bushels of table stock is just a little bit more than one-quarter of 1 per cent of their average production. But in the last few years they have been shipping more than 3 million bushels into our country, and this compares with an average annual production here of some 58 million bushels.
My study of the situation indicated that people generally from Prince Edward Island to British Columbia were concerned about this problem. They showed that in the concerted request they made to the tariff board. I should explain that Newfoundland was not represented, . and I can find no trace of Saskatchewan being represented.
In the hearing before the board there was talk of bigger acreage and that more machinery might be employed. It was suggested that large commercial growers using
mass production methods could meet United States competition without tariff changes. It was explained in the brief of the horticultural council representing Canada as a whole that less than 4 per cent of the registered United States growers harvest 77 per cent of the acreage and produce 91 per cent of the total crop. It was stated that generally

speaking the Canadian production is a part of the average farm program, although there are exceptions.
The statement was made to the board that in my own province the average grower has about 5 acres of potatoes. I think that is true, although there are exceptions of people who grow much more than that. I think there was fairly general agreement on the idea that we have to decide in this country the pattern of farm life we want not only to adopt but to keep. I think it was pretty generally agreed, too, that we should follow the family farm idea as much as possible. That was emphasized by people from my own province. I liked very much the reaction of Commissioner Leduc. Commenting on this phase of the discussion, he said:
It seems to me that you are fighting for a pattern of life-a pattern of agriculture. It is a pattern of life you are talking about, and I see the force of your argument because if you start to speculate the other way you do not know where you are going to stop. The only stopping place is Russia where you would have one producer . . . It is a way of life you are trying to protect and develop.
It was indicated to the tariff board that the average consumption of potatoes has fallen. Several reasons were given. I was interested in one particularly. It was said that the modern slimming trend comes into the picture. It was suggested that milady, with an eye on her figure, the hope that someone else would have an eye on it, has stopped eating potatoes. I find that Canadian consumption is 170 pounds per capita, while that of the United States is 100 pounds. It was stated at the hearing that there had been a sharp drop from 30 years ago. I looked into the problem and tried to find some statistics, but I could not find anything to indicate just what the consumption was 30 years ago.
I know the minister has taken this matter seriously. The fact that he ordered an investigation by the tariff board indicates that. I might say again that the people at home are very concerned about it, and they are asking for the most favourable and speedy treatment that is possible. Perhaps the minister may be able to make some statement at this time. I do not imagine the matter lends itself to speedy treatment, but I believe it would be helpful if we could have some indication of what is in the minister's mind with respect to this matter.
Mr. Chairman, I was thinking before I rose that it almost takes as much courage to speak on the last day as it does for a new member to make his first speech in the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Hear, hear.
Supply-Finance

I did not commence my first speech with generous congratulations to anyone, as apparently is the custom, so before I go on perhaps I might say that as one of the newest members here I have appreciated very much the way all hon. members have treated my remarks and the friendly spirit in which all parties have made me feel at home in the House of Commons.
I only intend to direct my remarks to one problem at this time. We in our group are very disappointed that again this year no plan has been provided to alleviate the rather unhappy position in which self-employed people find themselves in connection with providing some security for their old age. I think our record is quite clear with respect to this particular problem, because in reading Hansard of 1953 and 1954 I find that we set out very clearly that some relief should be given to this class of people. I am not going to repeat the arguments put forward in those two debates at great length, but I would refer hon. members to Hansard of April 10, 1953. pages 3702 to 3708 and Hansard of May 18, 1954, pages 4858 to 4863.
Here is a class of people who more than any other group in the country can, I suppose, be classified as a free enterprise group. It includes storekeepers, fishermen, farmers and professional groups of all kinds. We have seen a steady progression in legislation benefiting people so far as making some plans for their old age is concerned, but at no stage of development has there been any provision for income tax exemption in the case of those who are self-employed covering their contributions toward a retirement scheme as is allowed to ordinary employees. I think the arguments against some type of consideration for this group were very ably summed up from the standpoint of the defence by Mr. Abbott, the predecessor of the present Minister of Finance.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: On a point of order, I think I am quite within both my rights and the privileges of the committee in pointing out that this subject was raised during the budget debate and surely should not be the subject of a second debate. I know that on the administration item of my department one could presumably criticize my own conduct but, I should think, in connection with administration and not in connection with taxation matters that have been settled by resolutions and bills of the house.

Mr. Chairman, I certainly think the matter could be considered to be in order, since in the first item which we are now considering we find a reference to an amount set aside to cover the
6S24

Supply-Finance
administration of employees' instalment purchase plan and employees' group insurance plans.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: There is nothing in the item for self-employed people.

That may be quite true, but surely if we are in a position at this time to debate the efficacy of a type of plan provided for people who are employed by the government of Canada, we should also be in a position to debate whether the government should make some provision for those who cannot qualify under such a plan as set out in this item.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
On the point of order raised by the Minister of Finance, I would express the opinion that if the hon. member for York West is criticizing the administration by the Department of Finance of an existing act he is in order. But if he is recommending a change in the substantive law of the country; if he is recommending that something be there which has not yet been put there, and therefore which cannot have been mishandled by the Department of Finance, then there is not any administration which he can discuss under this question.
I think it is only fair to say that the hon. member did me the honour of asking me on what item this matter should be brought up. I had noticed that there was a reference in the administration item to the administration of employees' instalment purchase plans and employees' group insurance plans. But I pointed out that if this referred solely to plans dealing with employees of the government, then the discussion would have to be restricted to them.
I think the Minister of Finance is correct in stating that a discussion would be out of order at the present time, when the hon. member seeks to raise a point which could be adjusted only by budgetary action and not by departmental administration. If that is so, then with some regret I must suggest to the hon. member that his discussion comes too late in this session.

Do I gather that the tenor of my remarks would be admissible if I were criticizing in some respect the action of the minister in his capacity as Minister of Finance in not recommending some type of change in the Income Tax Act which would provide for this type of person? Is that in effect what the chairman is saying? Or am I prevented from criticizing in any way the administration of the minister's department in connection with this particular subject?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Perhaps I might make a suggestion, one which I trust will not be accepted as a precedent. It is that if the hon. member were to state briefly the point he wishes to raise, by that time he would have raised it. And even though I might find it necessary to rule it out of order, I suggest that at this late stage of the session it might be done. But I would not want to be held to it as a precedent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
On the point of order; since you were consulted, Mr. Chairman, I would not wish to intervene at all. Had I known that, I would not have spoken. On the other hand I think it is fair to the hon. member to say that he is quite aware of the situation, and that our general debates throughout the session-debates on the speech from the throne and the budget-give full scope for proposing to the government those schemes which are not presently adopted; and those are the occasions when such proposals can be made. Indeed, as I have pointed out, they were made in the debate on the budget, because I recall discussing the matter with the hon. member for St. Paul's.
I think it is quite correct to say that on these items I can be criticized only with respect to the administration of those statutes which I am charged with the responsibility of administering, and not those which the hon. member would like to have on the statute books. Nevertheless, as I have said, I hope the hon. member will be brief in what he says, particularly since he consulted with Your Honour.

Perhaps when I opened my remarks I should not have been so generous in what I said. If I had added that I intended to take only ten minutes this particular issue might not have been raised.
To continue, I would refer hon. members to page 3703 of Hansard for 1952-53. I am not going to read what appears there, but I am going to say that the case for the defence was summed up by the minister's predecessor in office along three lines, and they were these. First of all, that there is a tendency to exaggerate the differences which may arise because of the concessions made to the employee under plans of this kind, which are not available to the employer. Secondly, there was the point that the employer who does set up a plan for himself, on which he is paying income tax, has the funds available to use for various purposes in cases of emergency. The last point made by the minister at that time was that of course this application for assistance came

from people who were represented by organizations, and what are we going to do if all persons wish to become involved in this type of plan?
First of all the minister did point out that in connection with the employer type plan, the self-employed type plan, deduction was allowed from income for any of the interest accrued in the plan, whereas in the employee type plan the employee had to pay interest on his investment in this type of protection.
Let me say this, that it would take many years before there would be any equality in connection with the saving by one method to the employer of the penalty imposed on the employee in the way of taxes on the interest on his money. As a matter of fact I think if we took a case where a deduction of $900 was allowed to the employee and we calculated interest on that deduction, it would probably take 15 years before the two parties would be placed in the same situation.
The second point which was argued against our stand was that the employer type annuity or plan placed an asset at the disposal of the employer, which was not the case with the employee. Funds in connection with the latter's plan were frozen, and he had not access to them. Surely that is a defective answer to this situation; because obviously if there are types of emergencies in the case of an employer, the funds which are required, in I would think by far the vast majority of cases, are required to continue or enhance or prolong his business which, in turn, provides employment for the various people working for him. If we are going to take that attitude, then of course we will dry up the source of employers, and there will not be many people to work for, unless it is the state.
In connection with the third argument against the position we have taken, that it would necessitate people being in an organization like a law society, a dental association or a medical association, I do not think that argument holds water either. I am sure that if this type of proposition were put before the free-enterprise insurance companies their group departments would certainly be in a position to provide coverage for any employer who desired to take part in such a plan.
Now it is a proposition, so far as we are concerned, of putting up a case for a group of people who do require assistance to provide for their old age. It is one of the cardinal principles on which we operate that if at all possible old age is something for which the individual himself should make
Supply-Finance
every effort to take care. We are attempting by various government measures to supply supplementary benefits to take up the slack for those who cannot provide during their lifetime for all they need. If that is so, then this or any other government should be taking very positive steps to ensure that all classes of people are put in a position to provide security for that time. And without repeating the arguments that have been made previously in connection with this matter, as the minister has said, what I have said today does echo some of the remarks of the hon. member for St. Paul's. It also repeats some of the arguments of the hon. members for Eglinton and Greenwood.
I would respectfully suggest to the minister that as he begins his second term in office, some consideration should be given to that group of people without whom this country could not have achieved the stature it has today.

I am sure we all listened with a great deal of interest to the 40-minute exposition of the hon. member for Lethbridge on monetary theories. Ninety-five per cent of his 40-minutes were spent in discussing monetary and fiscal policies and monetary and credit theories. I am certain all members, and especially when we sit as backbenchers in the opposition, appreciate the courtesy and forbearance of the Minister of Finance, in that he has not interrupted in any way whatsoever. That being so, sir, I hope the Minister of Finance will also give me the courtesy of a few minutes for a practical discussion of fiscal policy that can only come under his direction, and on the practical issue of fiscal policies that were impossible to discuss until the present time.
As Minister of Finance I am certain he would like to make known to this House of Commons and to the people of Canada what he has in mind to recommend to the government in view of the situation which has developed in Great Britain only this week. Canada is an exporting nation. Export is trade; but as Canada does not trade on a reciprocal trade basis but on a financial trade basis, the situation which has developed in the past two days is of the utmost importance. The man who can give us the greatest direction in Canada is the Minister of Finance. As long as the present situation exists in Great Britain, the man who is more responsible than any other man for the economy of Canada is the Minister of Finance.
As the minister undoubtedly knows, on Monday the London stock market had what was described as "black Monday". I think we all know of the orders issued by the chancellor of the exchequer, R. A. Butler, in

Supply-Finance
London that day. It can only be interpreted as meaning that in Great Britain inflationary profits are to be regulated. If we can go by press reports from London, because of the prosperity in Great Britain, they have to go on a financial basis which indicates that they must have even less in the way of imports related to exports. In other words Great Britain has to export more and consume less in order to live if the position of the pound sterling is to remain strong. This actually means, sir, that in Great Britain the declaration of Mr. Butler is that they have to lower their standard of living. Since Canada is dependent to a great extent on her exports to Great Britain I should like to ask the minister a direct question, because I think it is basically a matter of financial policy as far as this country is concerned and therefore comes under the Minister of Finance. Will the government of Canada at least in part come to the rescue of Great Britain and ship our Canadian goods and commodities, of which we have a surplus at the present time, in exchange for sterling credits while Great Britain has to go through this temporary- and, sir, I have every confidence in Great Britain; I think it is temporary-deflationary period? If not, does the financial policy of the government and of the minister mean that we in Canada are going to sit on our surpluses unless we can get payment in dollars?
I was very much disturbed by what I read in our Canadian press as to why this action had to be taken by Mr. Butler, the chancellor of the exchequer in Great Britain. I wish to quote very briefly a part of the report in the Globe and Mail of Tuesday, July 26. Mr. Butler is quoted as saying:
He set the background to his new emergency measures by explaining that Britain's very prosperity and increased production are at the root of the trouble.
There is an economic contradiction if I ever heard one. That is capitalism, but I am not going into that at the moment. He also said:
Too much was being bought at home. This meant increased imports which in turn had to be paid for by increased exports. But sufficient exports to close the gap were not forthcoming.
I am going to be completely honest; I am going to read the next paragraph, because this is what disturbed me.
Harold Wilson, a former Labour trade minister, accused Butler of worsening the balance of payments "by the frivolous way he has increased purchases of dollar commodities, such as grain, which could have been imported from sterling sources.
Sir, both the new regulations the chancellor of the exchequer has put into effect in Great Britain and the criticism of a former Labour minister that part of the difficulty
fMr. Winch.]
was caused by the frivolous purchase of goods from dollar countries, should bring home to us right now a very serious situation and one on which, even before this House of Commons closes, we should have an understanding from the minister who is in charge of our financial obligations and relationships.
As to the position of Canada, we can only live by exports. If countries to whom we export goods, because of their monetary situation, have to bring in regulations so they cannot take our exports, then the situation in those countries is detrimental to the standard of living of the people of our own Dominion of Canada. I do believe, sir, that means that we should have now a clear understanding as to whether the situation from the point of view of international monetary matters is being studied by the government and the minister, and whether he has anything to recommend.
At the last session we heard a great deal about the convertibility of sterling. We have heard a little at this present session. I admit that I am not a financial economist, but the entire matter has interested me. In view of this situation I was most interested to receive a copy of a communication signed by Sir Edward C. G. Boyle, who is the economic secretary to the treasury in the House of Commons in Great Britain, dealing with what an individual or a corporation in a Canadian dollar area can do if he is selling into a sterling area such as Great Britain. I want to quote briefly from it. I am not going to take 40 minutes as my hon. friend did. In brief, as far as Canada is concerned, this is the situation:
(a) Sterling earned by a resident of the dollar area, i.e. the American account area and Canada may be used:
(i)	to make payments in the sterling area;
(ii)	to make payments to any country outside the sterling area;
(iii)	to Pay for sterling area goods shipped to any country in the world;
(iv)	to acquire dollars on demand from a United Kingdom bank at a current market rate, or from any bank in the dollar area who is a buyer of sterling;
(v)	to purchase gold in the London market from authorized dealers.
I understand that because of its economic position Great Britain has been buying great quantities of gold from the U.S.S.R. and paying for it in sterling. They are prepared to pay in sterling or in gold; at least that is the interpretation I place on this letter from the economic secretary to the treasury in Great Britain.
Canada could have increased her trade with Great Britain in the past, or may be able to increase her trade at the present time, if we operated on a triangular trade basis. Perhaps I could explain that to hon. members who

may not know what I am driving at. We have been buying quantities of butter and cheese from New Zealand, which is in the sterling area. As I understand this information, we could ship to Great Britain, purchase from New Zealand or any other sterling area country and utilize our sterling credits from our exports to Great Britain to pay for our purchases in sterling rather than in dollars.
I am not going into the details, as I am sure the minister is conversant with the seriousness of this situation. I am convinced that Canada has a responsibility in what is now a time of trial and tribulation for Great Britain which once again has to go on something like an austerity program. We have the surpluses which Great Britain needs but which she cannot take. Mr. Butler said last Monday that she cannot take them because they have no Canadian dollars. Surely Canada as a part of the commonwealth could work out deals on some basis. Surely Canada with her love for the mother country will make our surpluses available during this time of need, and not demand dollars. We should be able to work within the five points set out by the treasury in Great Britain and utilize credits on sterling payments.
I should like to talk at length on this matter, but I am not going to take advantage of this opportunity to do so. I appreciate the minister giving me an opportunity to speak, and I hope he will be able to give us some indication that a study will be made of this problem which is facing our greatest market; and it is hoped he can work out some method whereby Canada can export and assist our mother country.

Mr. Chairman, I want to take only a minute or two to endorse the remarks made by the hon. member for Queens regarding the tariff on potatoes coming into this country. I was particularly pleased to notice that the minister gave signs of approval, at least of the speech if not the subject of the speech, by applauding on his desk.
We on the Pacific coast are faced with the same problem confronting the maritime provinces. Early potatoes come into Vancouver and Victoria from California just as our own early potatoes are reaching the local markets. If the date on which the tariff is applied could be advanced say to May 1 it would be of great assistance to the potato growers on Vancouver island. I imagine the same thing would apply to the potato growers in the Ashcroft district in the interior of British Columbia, although I am not as familiar with that district as I am with Vancouver island. Within the last few weeks I have had complaints from potato growers who say that once again their market is being destroyed by early potatoes coming in
Supply-Finance
from California. Perhaps the solution may be to advance the date upon which the tariff is made applicable.

Mr. Chairman, I do not think I shall take very long, but I have a matter to discuss that pertains to two different things. I suppose you could call it a matter of internal economy. It constitutes what might, be called a physical block or a fixation which is seeking release. Very few people seem to want to have anything to do with this matter, which concerns employees who work for the government.
These employees are grouped in certain categories. There are those who are seasonal and sessional, there are those who are permanent and there are those who are called permanent temporaries. I suppose you could classify seasonal and sessional employees who are fortunate enough to have year-round employment as permanent temporaries, while those who are seasonal and sessional could be classified as part-time employees.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I point out that that is the responsibility of the civil service commission.
It has to do with superannuation. That is what I am working up to.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: If the hon. member will confine himself to superannuation I shall be glad to discuss it.
This comes under page 202 of the details.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Which is superannuation.

Statutory payments under the superannuation and retirement acts; that is what I am getting up to. I realize that I am probably on difficult ground, but if you will bear with me I shall not take too long. Whether or not it comes up under this item it will come up eventually, and I think it will be in the interests of all concerned to take it into consideration now.
I refer to the possibility of giving some consideration to employees who are retired because of age. Some of these employees do not get the consideration that they are entitled to. Many of them have worked for the government for 20 or 25 years. If they are not in the category of permanent employees, or seasonal or sessional or what you call permanent temporaries, they do not receive the same consideration. Permanent temporary employees get the full benefit of retirement leave as well as sick leave, but while the seasonal and sessional employees get sick leave, if they do not use it up during the year it is not accumulated. The

Supply-Finance
permanent and permanent temporary employees have the benefit of enjoying cumulative sick leave on the same basis as the full-time employee.
I think the minister realizes that we cannot say much about it now, but if a committee were appointed representative of all parties of the house it could take up this matter in respect to these individuals. It is something they cannot take up themselves. It is one of those unfortunate situations which very few members want to take up because it is not a pleasant task.
There is a grievance. There is an inequality which I do not think the members of this house want to see exist. A committee of all parties of this house should take up the matter with the' different departments, as it applies to almost every department; but particularly the Speaker's department. Under the circumstances the Minister of Finance should try to rectify this by adjusting the whole matter to the satisfaction of the staff who are unfairly if not unjustly dealt with.
I should like very briefly to support the hon. member who has just spoken with respect to superannuation arrangements for sessional employees.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Of this house?
That is the subject the previous member was speaking about.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am not responsible for the House of Commons.

But I should like to point out that the Minister of Finance's department can do something to correct this, because some of the employees have been in touch with the officials in his department. At the present time there is a certain injustice and a certain confusion. I should like to draw the minister's attention to the fact that first of all the employees received a letter from Mr. R. B. Bryce, clerk of the privy council, informing them of arrangements for contributions to the superannuation account. That letter is countersigned by Mr. Leonard Hill and is dated 5th of May. Then they received a letter dated July 1 from Mr. Leonard Hill with further instructions. Then they received another letter from Patrice F. Cyr with further instructions.
After receiving all this confusing correspondence, one or several of them decided to telephone some of the officials of the minister's department. They advised them that a few of these letters were not correct, so they were more confused than ever. In addition to that, you see the forms that had to be filled out. Here is one of them. They
(Mr. Small.]
are asked to complete these forms. On making inquiries of personnel about some points which were not quite clear, they were informed it was not necessary to complete this form at all because of a certified minute from the treasury board.
In addition there are certain things in connection with the form that seem rather stupid. They are asked to give the day they joined the service. That is rather difficult for some women who have been here 25 or 30 years and, I think, quite unnecessary. But my point in rising was to urge that fairness be shown to these sessional employees who have worked here many years and who under the present regulations cannot take advantage of superannuation. I would suggest that the minister have an official of the superannuation branch meet these employees to discuss with them all the facts concerning the superannuation plan, because they are completely confused and they can only have the situation made clear by one of his officials undertaking to deal directly with them.

Mr. Chairman, I shall be only a minute. I noticed the minister attempting to rise after the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary had spoken. I hope when he gives his reply in the house he will not neglect to answer the petition put forward.
It is a very serious situation. I have five municipal organizations in my riding. All of them are desperately in need of the operation of this fund. I should like to endorse the raising of the amount from $30 million to $100 million. The problem is becoming worse each year. If we look at what is being done by the Social Credit government of Alberta to aid its municipalities, the Liberal federal government would not want to have it said that it was able to give less aid to municipal financing than the Social Credit government of Alberta.

Mr. Chairman, I assure the Minister of Finance that I do not intend to engage, or to attempt to engage, in a full-dress debate at this time. I rise largely because I feel it is my responsibility, even though the hour is late and the minister wishes to get through, to put certain facts before him for his consideration.
The minister is a new Minister of Finance. I consider him to be one of the bright minds of our country. I am not attempting to flatter him. I have known and admired the minister for some time. I have associated with him in various ways, and I have great confidence in his ability to look facts in the face. I would dearly love at this time to be able to

get the minister into a full-scale debate on his financial policy. However, the hour is late and it would be unwise perhaps for me to do so, but let me say that no one is to blame but the minister himself for not having had his estimates before the house earlier than this so we could engage in a full-scale debate on financial policy.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: He has been unselfish.

He has been self-effacing and unselfish in helping the other cabinet members get their estimates through, and he is the kind of person who would wait until the last minute to get his own through. At the same time we like occasionally to have an opportunity for a full-dress debate on financial policy. We asked his predecessor on several occasions to allow us such an opportunity. His predecessor, who was a most affable man, did say, "Next session we shall try to make an opportunity''. That opportunity never came. I am hoping the present Minister of Finance will see fit-in fact, will feel it is his responsibility-to provide an opportunity for such a full-dress debate on his financial policy at the earliest possible time. As I say, I hope he will, but just in case he does not-
Would the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.
Does he still hope that the finance estimates will come in any year on anything but the last hour of the last day?

I suppose that is naive of me, and perhaps it is the triumph of hope over experience, but I still have hope, and I am pleading with my hon. friend the minister to be wise enough at another session to give us that opportunity. .
I might tell him that I am actuated by two inducements at this moment to say a few words about his policy. The first inducement is this. The Ottawa Journal of May 31 of this year carried an editorial calling upon members of parliament to stay on the job until the unemployment problem was solved. We have not solved it by any means. It looks as if we are close to prorogation, and we shall not be on the job to solve it. But I believe the major factor in the solution of the unemployment problem in this country is financial and monetary. Because I believe that, I certainly am not doing my full duty toward the Canadian people and discharging my responsibility to them if I do not at this time bring before the minister and his colleague, the Minister of Justice, certain things I would like them to study and consider during the period between now and the next session.
Supply-Finance
For the information of the hon. member for Greenwood, if the minister does not bring his estimates down early next year, it will be my determination to bring in either a bill or a resolution which will make it necessary for him to debate his financial policy on something other than his own estimates, and I believe we shall be doing the country a service by having that sort of thing.
I couple the Minister of Justice with my friend the Minister of Finance because I see him in the house today, and I would want him to hear what I have to say. I hope he will do me the honour of listening for just a minute or two. I know that he is an extremely busy man, but I am sure he can spare just a few minutes to listen to what I have to say.
I want to say this to my hon. friend, and it is completely in connection with the financial policy of the country. His colleague the Minister of Justice recently paid us a visit in the province of Alberta. We were glad to have him. It was a good thing, and we welcomed him as best we could. He was there, of course, attempting to justify the policy of the Minister of Finance by telling the people, "What is the use of attempting to send back from this particular constituency a Social Credit member? Why do you not send a Liberal?" That was all right. It was his privilege to do that.
Was he speaking to the Canadian Club?

No, he was speaking to an extremely interested audience in a constituency called Battle River-Camrose. He was trying to tell the people why it would be wise to send a Liberal and not a Social Crediter down here. In the course of his remarks he made a statement which I think should bear some examination. If he is reported correctly in the press he said, "No top-ranking economist has ever endorsed the Social Credit proposals."

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is correct.

The minister nods his head and says that is correct. Hansard does not record a nod either this way or that way. For that reason I felt that we should describe the nod. He made a statement which I think should be made in a forum where he can be answered. I could not be on the same platform with him because I was not invited to the Liberal meeting, but I can be with him in the House of Commons.
I am now going to say this to the Minister of Justice, and I am trying to be as calm and reasonable with him as possible. I am going to say to him now that he has a wonderful opportunity right now, during the discussion of these estimates, to stand up on the floor of this house

Supply-Finance
and debate that question. I am going to give him a little bit of homework to do. I maintain that the minister was completely wrong and uninformed, and that because he was wrong and uninformed he misdirected the jury which was composed of the voters of Battle River-Camrose. They realized, of course, that they were being misdirected and did not take his advice. But my comment is that he overlooked-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I admit that they were misdirected, because they elected a Social Credit candidate by a very narrow margin.

I said they were misdirected by the Minister of Justice, Mr. Chairman, and that is the contention I make today. That is the subject I want to discuss just briefly. To my hon. friend who perhaps has not had time to go into these things, let me point out what Social Credit proposals are, first in the financial field.
Write us a letter.

Of course if my hon. friend wishes me to take a great deal of time I can do it. But if he is going to leave on this afternoon's train I can write him a letter, as he suggests. But I want to talk to my friend the Minister of Justice for a moment and to my friend the Minister of Finance. I am taking their proposition, not mine.
As I said, what is the Social Credit financial proposal? It can be divided into three simple parts. The first one is this. We claim there is ample evidence to show that the production of goods and services today does not distribute amongst the consumers of Canada sufficient purchasing power to enable the people to buy back what they produce and that, as a consequence, there will be generated a shortage of purchasing power.
The second part of it is this. If our productive processes generate a deficiency of purchasing power, then there must be some means of making up the deficiency and we propose that, as a mechanism for making up that deficiency, some agency of government shall create and distribute amongst the consumers of Canada new purchasing power equal to the deficiency that has been generated so there will be a balance between consumption and production.
The third important feature of it, Mr. Chairman, is this. The mechanism by which that shall be done shall be the Bank of Canada coupled with the treasury of Canada -that is the Department of Finance-and we propose that they unite in their efforts to see that the new purchasing power is distributed in sufficient quantity to balance consumption with production. That in a nutshell is the financial proposal we make.

I cited that proposal, Mr. Chairman, because I wanted first to make it known to the committee exactly what it is we hold as a fundamental principle, and so I can then cite top-ranking economists who not only advocate the same thing but who, through their long study of economies throughout the world, have discovered exactly the same thing that Major Douglas discovered away back about 1922 or 1923.
First, for my friend the Minister of Justice, and in order to refute completely what he said, I am going to cite one of the top-ranking economists of the United States, who for 18 years was head of the department of economics at Texas University. I am speaking of Professor C. E. Ayres. After a long study of the economy of the United States, which operates on exactly the same principles of finance as those upon which we operate, Professor Ayres came to certain conclusions which he embodied in a book published in 1946 and entitled "The Divine Right of Capital". At pages 32 and 33, where he is discussing the habit of pendulum thinking that people have got into, or the habit of thinking in terms of booms and busts, he says this:
There are some in whom this habit-
That is the habit of pendulum thinking. -still persists today and who are therefore already talking of the depression which will "inevitably" follow post-war inflation, which with admirable consistency they also think of as inevitable.
But pendulum thinking is not as common as it was. We have learned a lot since 1929. Obviously that is because we have seen a lot. So long as disturbances are kept within decent bounds, economists prefer to view them with Olympian detachment, taking a "long-run" view of upward and downward movements and not worrying too much about incidental "friction". But when the friction generates heat so intense that it threatens to blow the whole outfit galleywest, most of us are strongly moved to stop, look and listen.
What we have learned as a result-
I suppose, if I may interpolate, from stopping, looking and listening.
-now seems obvious indeed. The economic heretics-
I suppose they would be the Social Crediters.
-have been trying all along to make us see it. No economy could swing back and forth so wildly from one extreme to the other without there being something very wrong about it. There is indeed something very wrong with ours. It fails to distribute mass-consumer purchasing power in sufficient quantity to permit the entire product of industry to be purchased. This failure exists at all times under capitalism and is noxious at all times.
That is a statement in succinct terms of the first part of the financial principle which I put forward as the Social Credit principle a few moments ago. Here is a top-ranking

economist making the same statement, an economist who is accepted very widely. But let me ask the Minister of Justice this question. Can you, sir, picture a man sitting for 18 years in the top economic seat in one of the great universities of the United States unless he had something on the ball, unless he was pretty widely accepted? I cannot, and I do not think the Minister of Justice can.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think my hon. friend could solve this matter very quickly if he would give the members of the committee the name of some top-ranking economist anywhere in the world who has specifically endorsed the doctrines of Social Credit as such.
I am doing that right now.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Your merely saying that your ideas are like his does not constitute an endorsement by him of Social Credit.

It is not a case of saying that our ideas are like his. What I am saying is that here is a man who in his investigations has discovered exactly the proposition which Major Douglas, the founder of Social Credit, put forward; and the fact that he did not by accident mention Social Credit in his thesis is no justification for my hon. friend saying that no top-ranking economist has ever endorsed it. If he endorses the principle, then he endorses Social Credit because that is a Social Credit principle.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: You are just saying that he does.

I am quoting to you from his own work, and I shall go further. I remind my hon. friend that the second part of my Social Credit proposition was this, that wherever it is discovered that there is a deficiency of purchasing power generated within the economy, then the remedy for it is a flow of new purchasing power sufficient to make it possible for consumers to buy what is being produced. Does he endorse that principle? Let us see if he does. I turn to page 95 in this same book by the same author, Professor C. E. Ayres, head of the economics department of Texas University. This is what he says in chapter 17:
What we require, and all we require, to make the industrial economy work is a flow of mass-consumer purchasing power sufficient to absorb the entire product of industry at whatever level of production we may be able to achieve. This would not bring Utopia. It would not solve all problems. On the contrary, it would solve only one problem, the crisis into which we have been thrust by the institutions and dogmas of absolute capitalism. But this problem is the most important one we face today in this sense. If we solve this problem, we shall then have an opportunity to tackle others.
Supply-Finance
If We do not, all our present problems will merge in the general collapse of the present structure of western society.
There is an endorsement without qualification of the second part of our thesis. I shall turn to another very quickly, and tell the minister that here is another first-ranking economist who has endorsed exactly the same principle. Here is the president of the University of New Mexico in a book entitled, "Financing Full Employment". It was published in 1945 and the author is Dr. J. Philip Wernette. A man holding such a prominent position and writing on economic policies and matters would have to be a topranking economist to be able to hold his position as president of that university in the face of the criticism that his books and publications would evoke. I shall refer to what he said in his book entitled, "Financing Full Employment", and I want the members of the committee, particularly the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Justice, who has been engaging in a sort of Dutch battle and not coming to grips with us, to listen to what this man has to say. I challenge the minister to take up the debate; to not merely ridicule what is said but bring something before us to show that he has the facts. Dr. Wernette had this to say:
Control of the total amount of money must be assumed by the government and exercised through a federal stabilization board. This board shall have power to create new money to be used in financing deficits in the federal budget and in paying off the federal debt. The board, guided by reliable statistics on employment, unemployment and other economic factors, shall issue such new money in whatever amounts may be necessary any time that depression threatens, so as directly and indirectly to stimulate and maintain employment at a practical maximum.
That, Mr. Chairman, is a 100 per cent endorsement of the technique which we have been putting forward in this country for the last 30 years and which the Minister of Justice evidently has not yet looked into very carefully. I might point out for the benefit of my Conservative friends that back in 1930 Winston Churchill had been giving this matter some thought, and he made this statement:
There is a strange discord between consuming and producing power, a mysterious crack between supply and demand upon which the keenest minds in the world should be concentrated.
That was Winston Churchill's view.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, could I ask my hon. friend if he regards Sir Winston Churchill as one of the supporters of Social Credit?

No, and I have not said so. I have
merely quoted him. The thing that induced me to use that statement of Sir Winston Churchill was that it recognized the thing

Supply-Finance
which the Minister of Justice refuses to recognize and which he should be recognizing if he is to give this country the service which it requires at his hands. If the Minister of Finance is to serve this country as I know he wants to serve it, then he will induce his colleague the Minister of Justice to study these matters so they will know-and I think they will recognize that it is their responsibility to see to it-that production and purchasing power are geared together in this country.
I am sure the Minister of Finance must recognize that today the issuing of new money is a haphazard business, and the more he looks into it the more he will discover that is so; that there is no control whatsoever from day to day, from month to month or year to year of the amount of money that is issued into circulation to buy goods and services that Canadians produce. I am certain that if they will give the matter some study they will find that it is necessary to concentrate the very best minds in our country upon the problem of balancing consumption with production.
I suggest to the Minister of Finance that since the Gordon commission has been set up to investigate the economy of Canada, one of the responsibilities which should devolve upon it is to investigate this very matter. If he will do that I think he will come back here at the next session and get up before the house and say he has discovered that what these boys have been saying all these years is right, and they are going to change the situation.
Six o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: If I may be permitted a word for a moment, I take it that the general debate has ended.
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No one rose.
I said it was six o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am going to deal with that in a moment.
I have dealt with it now.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Then would the committee consider resuming at seven o'clock rather than eight?
No.
Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Finance had his fling last night and early this morning. It is six o'clock.

I am not thinking of that, but I am thinking of the staff again. I am thinking particularly of the Hansard staff and the stenographers, who have been working continuously. I think while we might be

quite fresh and willing to sit at seven o'clock, we should not impose that upon the people who have been working under such pressure for the last day or so. I believe we should meet as usual at eight o'clock.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. Resolution 112; shall this resolution carry?

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
General administration-
113. Comptroller of the treasury-central office and branch offices administration, $15,616,300.
Is the minister going to reply?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes, on item 113. A number of statements have been made, and if I miss any of them I hope I shall be reminded of it. Let me take them in turn. The hon. member for Broadview-
For Greenwood.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The hon. member for Greenwood-the hon. member for Broadview has assured me he has made his last speech in the house and I would not suggest that he is going to make another one-covered three points. First was the question of the treasury board, which we went into in some detail in the committee, and its influence or authority with respect to the spending of other departments, and with particular reference to an investigation by outside persons into the efficiency of the administration of other departments. I would not want the hon. member to hold the view that he tries to tell the committee he holds, that the treasury board would not have some influence in these matters.
It is the duty of the treasury board to supervise in many ways not only the preparation of the estimates but various factors that enter into the hiring of persons, the providing of the establishment, the salary range and all these things that are directly under the control of the civil service commission, that are nevertheless the responsibility of the Minister of Finance in so far as expenditures are concerned. Therefore treasury board does in fact, through the Minister of Finance, exercise an influence, if you like, or express an opinion with respect to many of the financial aspects of government in the other departments. When I said "treasury board" I referred, of course, in fact to the staff and not to the treasury board as a cabinet committee.
To say that the staff might impose upon another department an investigation of its

affairs, of its establishment, of its pay list and all these things, is going somewhat beyond what one would expect. However, the treasury board officials, in consultation with the officials of the other departments, of course, try to improve the efficiency of government on all occasions; and if perchance it is felt an investigation of some particular matter is called for, the treasury board officials themselves may participate in such a study with the officials of the other department and perhaps in fact on many occasions clear the matter up immediately without further ado.
As I said in the estimates committee, this is a daily grist. This goes on the year round. That is what treasury board officials are for; that is how they earn their pay that the government gives them. If, however, my hon. friend supposes that even the Minister of Finance could arbitrarily decide that there should be and would be an investigation such as he has in mind, of course he would understand that would be impossible. That is a matter of government policy, a matter of government decision, a matter of consideration and examination and decision not only by the treasury board itself, the Minister of Finance and the appropriate minister, but even perhaps the cabinet itself. All these steps have been taken in the past and no doubt will be taken in the future should the occasion arise when those persons concerned feel it necessary.
The hon. member gave a short rehearsal of the economic factors involved in the budget, and asked me whether I was under the influence of some of the persons who have studied at the feet of a man by the name of Keynes. I do not think I ought to go into that. I have never inquired of any of my officials or of my colleagues as to their views on that point. In fact if I asked them what their views were they would probably give me qualifications that would only confuse the issue. What we want is a decision at budget time about what is necessary and desirable at that particular time, without trying to adhere to a theory of any preceding period. I mention that only to say that of course it is out of order in this debate.
The hon. members for Queens and Esqui-malt-Saanich were kind enough to make some reference to the proceedings before the tariff board with respect to potatoes. Since we have originated the reference I think I need only say here that we did originate it because of representations which had been made to us especially by the maritime potato growers, and having in mind the changed market conditions which were referred to by the hon. member for Queens.
Supply-Finance
We feel that if there is a substantial change in market conditions, and if representations are made which have validity, a reference of the particular matter to the tariff board is the best way in which we can have a study made by experts who will place before us the facts of the situation. I can assure the hon. member for Queens that the maritime potato growers, when they came here in the spring, made a case for reference to the tariff board and we acted upon it. The results in so far as the study is concerned will have to do with the potato growers on Vancouver island as well.
The hon. member for Okanagan Boundary, followed by the hon. member for Yale and I think the hon. member for Fraser Valley, sought to intervene to speak on the subject of the Municipal Improvements Assistance Act, which was passed in 1938. It was an unemployment assistance provision, designed to stimulate the building of municipal services at a time when employment was needed. The terms, of course, were generous; but it should be remembered that the provincial governments had to guarantee the loan which was made by the federal government to the municipality. The last loans we made under this act were in 1940, because it may be recalled that during the war years the municipalities and the provincial governments co-operated with the federal government in postponing as much as they could any municipal services or any other buildings of a strictly nonessential nature. When the war years were over the situation was not that credit was needed from this source, but that the municipalities could and did in fact finance nearly as they chose. We think that condition has obtained until recently.
However, I have been informed that in recent weeks representations have been made that some municipalities find it difficult to get money. Without arguing the question as to whether their condition was such that it might be impossible for them to get money or whether the particular project was one for which they normally could not borrow money, may I say that these representations have been made and I have been studying the Municipal Improvements Assistance Act since last fall, somewhat as an academic study but nevertheless in connection with the discussions which we will be having in October with the provincial governments under the heading of public investment.
Is the act still in force, and is the $30 million still available?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
We have not the $30 million. The provision was that we could lend up to $30 million. Should we do anything at the

Supply-Finance
moment by way of using the powers under the act it would be necessary to vote the money required for the project.
But the act is still in force?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The act is on the statute books, yes. Because of what I have said, namely that this might come under the heading of public investment in October, I choose not to say anything more than to assure hon. members that we are aware of the act, we are aware of the low interest rate which was offered to municipal corporations at that time, and no doubt this and other similar subjects will be discussed in October.
The minister says the money is not available and would have to be voted, but I understand that in the original vote there was an allocation of $30 million.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
What I said was that if we chose to lend money under the act to municipal corporation X we would have to vote the amount of the loan, just as we would vote money to lend it to the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation or for any of these other loans we make.
The hon. member for Peace River was kind enough to say that he would not engage in a debate on monetary fiscal policy this evening but would postpone his remarks until the next session. Of course he then went on to tease us a little by giving us a preview of what those remarks might be. Let me say in his absence that I am sure we can look forward to a discussion of monetary policies by him in the coming session. Perhaps by that time I shall have an opportunity to study the book to which he referred and the authority referred to, and any other authorities which may be referred to by him in the meantime.
I think the same would apply to the remarks of the hon. member for Lethbridge, who repeated the argument he has made before in the house with regard to subsidies for local industries and activities. I was a little surprised that he should think the Minister of Finance would be enamoured with the idea of subsidies; nevertheless he made the proposal in the light of a general over-all approach to the welfare of Canada.
