I might just add that I am not prepared to agree with him that the government of Canada should find money for subsidies for this purpose, but at the same time I would point out that we do provide subsidies for the coal industry, for the gold mining industry and in a somewhat different manner than he had in mind we provide subsidies for feed grain moving to the east. He had in mind a subsidy for local industries to allow them to compete with the products of the central

provinces. We are doing precisely the same thing, only in reverse, with respect to feed grains. He may argue from this that, the principle having been accepted, we ought to do many other things. All I can say is that I shall look forward to his discussion of monetary policies next year; but let me say that as Minister of Finance it will be difficult to convince me that we ought to pay more subsidies.
I think that concludes the references to what has been said today, except what was said by the hon. member for Vancouver East. In that connection may I refer to the trade figures with the United Kingdom. Without going into detail, may I give our exports to the United Kingdom in the first five months of this year as compared with the same period last year. Our exports from January 1 to May 31, 1954, were some $234 million, while for the like period this year they were $321 million, roughly $80 million more this year than last. That does not indicate the state of affairs which my hon. friend had in mind when he was concerned about the export of Canadian goods to the United Kingdom.

I was referring to the announcement by the chancellor of the exchequer, who said they did not have Canadian or United States dollars. I was not referring to the past, but to what is going to happen from now on.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
In that connection I would point out to the committee that the chancellor of the exchequer gave no indication of any quotas or restrictions other than those now in existence. In his announcement, and in the speech made in the House of Commons, he did not forecast any restrictions on imports from Canada. If I might run over what he did say just to clarify my hon. friend's mind, he referred to restrictions on consumer credit and instalment buying. He referred to certain restrictions on bank loans in the United Kingdom. He referred to a reduction in government expenditures on capital goods. He stated specifically that there was no crisis of any kind but that there had been a slight reduction in the gold reserves of the United Kingdom. The only action he had in mind was as I have mentioned already.
There is nothing there which indicates in any way action which would reduce the purchasing power of the United Kingdom with respect to Canadian goods. My hon. friend may say that may be so. The fact is that we have been through this before, but at the moment we can expect no action to be taken by the chancellor of the exchequer, certainly not as a result of his speech the

other day with respect to the sale of Canadian goods in the United Kingdom.

One hot day last week the minister was kind enough to offer to make a calculation over the week end to find out how many hours had been lost by civil servants during the hot weather this summer, and also how large a down payment that amount would have made on some air conditioning equipment.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I did tell my hon. friend I would try to find out, but I have been told it would be somewhat difficult. As I reminded him the other day, the decision is in the hands of the deputy minister of the department concerned. I have been told by my own deputy that during this summer the amount of time lost by the Department of Finance staff in the Confederation building, he thinks, is about three-quarters of an hour on four or five occasions. However, I would have to go over each of the departments concerned, find out what buildings they were in and whether or not there was air conditioning there, make quite a lengthy study and probably end up with no better answer.

Some of the offices closed as early as one o'clock. It seems to me that if it were suggested that in the winter we stop buying coal to cut down expenses, people would think there was something wrong with the running of our country. When we build new buildings such as the veterans affairs building and the new library, it is very difficult to justify the fact that we cannot find the material and the manpower to instal air conditioning. At some point we should know what the total estimated loss is because of our failure to have this very convenient device. I understand that Loblaws are opening a $500,000 building in Ottawa tomorrow, and the Loblaw firm considers it good business to have the establishment air conditioned. I think we should have some estimate.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I should be glad to go further into the matter from the standpoint of savings, but I have complete confidence in the decision made by my colleague the Minister of Public Works when it comes to the constructing of buildings, the cost of installation of air conditioning and similar matters.

The Minister of Trade and Commerce has indicated that it is government policy that air conditioning should not be used in government buildings. It would appear to me that would become a cabinet responsibility. As I said before, I do not think any government would argue that it should not have heating in buildings in Canada, or that we should close our buildings for the
Supply-Finance
wintertime. I think it is just as senseless to argue that Canada cannot afford to make use of the air conditioning industry, which is a legitimate industry, and start using it in new construction like the new veterans affairs building.
I think the Minister of Finance is the minister to look into the cost factor and find out what the loss is to the Canadian treasury to have 50,000 or 75,000 civil servants go home at one o'clock, two o'clock or three o'clock for the rest of the day, day after day. At some point some department of government should be able to tell us how many thousand hours have been lost this summer. It may take until next year to get that information. I thought that as the minister had a week's notice, he might be able to give us some information.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: We have made efforts, as I said, and we shall continue to do so in the hope of having some concrete figures for this summer.

I am very much interested in the subject of air conditioning in our buildings in Ottawa, and I appreciate the endeavours of my hon. friend; but under this item I am more interested in the trade carried out with sterling countries. Would the minister enlarge on what he said a few moments ago? As I understood the remarks of the Minister of Finance, in spite of the devaluation in Great Britain he does not expect any impact on the export business of Canada. That is what I understood from the minister, but I cannot believe he meant what he said. The economic and financial impact of what the chancellor of the exchequer has had to do in Great Britain cannot help being detrimental to the export trade of Canada. How can the minister say it is not going to have such an effect?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: My hon. friend begins with a misunderstanding of what the chancellor said. He did not announce a devaluation of the pound.
I agree with that, but it is a devaluation in Great Britain because of the orders that have been put in-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The orders to which I referred a moment ago were orders with respect to restrictions on instalment buying. That is as my hon. friend knows, down payments on goods have been increased. That may or may not restrict purchasing power. It probably will; at least the chancellor hopes it will. However, it will prevent more credit being granted for the time being. That does not necessarily mean they will not buy Canadian grain, because one does not buy Canadian grain on credit; one buys it for cash. The bank loans in the United Kingdom which

Supply-Finance
are to be restricted, or perhaps not granted quite as easily, would be loans made to local firms. They may not be buying Canadian goods for resale in the United Kingdom. These things, of course, may possibly prevent someone from buying something from Canada, but in itself there is nothing here to restrict purchases of Canadian goods as the ordinary practices are now. If, however, the chancellor were to announce additional quotas on Canadian goods, then my hon. friend's position would be correct.

Could I ask only one more question, and then I shall sit down. From all the press reports I have read, not only in Canadian newspapers but also in those of Great Eritain, it is my interpretation that this is being done mainly because they are short of United States and particularly of Canadian dollars. Would the minister state whether or not it is a shortage of Canadian dollars that is having an effect in Great Britain? Everything I have read in the Canadian press-and I take in all the press of Canada-indicates that it is because they are short of Canadian dollars. If they are short of Canadian dollars they cannot take our goods. Am I right or am I wrong in my interpretation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: You are wrong, if I may say so with respect.

Then will you make it clear, which the chancellor has not done? Every article I have read indicates that they have to do this because they are short of Canadian dollars. That is why I asked this afternoon if we could not help from Canada in the matter of sterling payments.

On the point raised by the hon. member for Vancouver East, I think the Minister of Finance will appreciate that this matter is of great interest and importance to the people of British Columbia, particularly those connected with our basic industries of forest products and fishing. Would the minister not agree that it was on that premise of the shortage of Canadian dollars that the trade mission from the British Columbia fishing industry went to Britain, in order to canvass the possibilities of increasing our purchases of British products so they might more freely dispose of their fisheries products in Britain?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I agree that they went over to see if they could sell more goods. But in general we have had no difficulty in the past year with quotas or restrictions. Perhaps my hon. friend would be interested to know that one can sell

Canadian wheat, Canadian lumber and Canadian base metals in the United Kingdom and the purchasers there can use Canadian dollars without restrictions; there are no quotas whatever. There are quotas with respect to manufactured goods, that is, quotas on Canadian money with which to buy them; but Canadian raw products such as I have indicated may be imported into the United Kingdom under general licence without restriction. For that reason, as I tried to tell my friend the hon. member for Vancouver East, we are considering a situation that does not exist. Those who are thinking in terms of difficulty are thinking of a condition that existed up to 12, 14 or 18 months ago.

I am sorry to persist, but I am interested. If that is the case, why is it reported that the chancellor of the exchequer says they have to impose restrictions in Great Britain because they have not dollars?
I am interested. I am just seeking information.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I cannot explain what writers might say. I am trying to explain to the committee as best I can the announcement of the chancellor of the exchequer as I understood it to be. It may well turn out that I am wrong, but I assure my hon. friend that I find nothing in the statement which indicated an intention on his part to reimpose those restrictions which he had on imports from Canada until some time ago.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall resolution 113 carry?
Then why is it we are told that Britain cannot buy Canadian salmon and Canadian apples because she needs the dollars for the purchase of more essential commodities? That is what we are told.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Perhaps I did not make myself quite clear when my hon. friend was not in the chamber.
I was here, but I was behind the curtain.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: When I read the items I read wheat, lumber, base metals.
But you did not say salmon.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It may be that they have always had restrictions on apples and salmon and may still have them. What I was trying to say to my friend the hon. member for Vancouver East was that there is nothing in this recent announcement which would indicate an extension of the quotas or restrictions that are at present in existence.
The quotas on apples and salmon are still there because they need the dollars to buy wheat, lumber and base metals.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Quite so.
So there are restrictions owing to a shortage of dollars.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Quite so.

I am not going to pursue this matter any further. I am grateful to the minister for the information he has given. When the estimates of the Secretary of State were before the house-and they included the civil service commission-I wanted to ask a question and the minister told me that I should ask it under the estimates of the Minister of Finance. I want to ask a question on this civil service insurance. Will the minister tell me whether or not I can ask the question now? If not, will he advise me under what item I may ask it? I held it over on the advice of the Secretary of State. Shall I ask it now?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: If the hon. member asks his question now I may have the answer by the time we reach the appropriate item.

Thank you. What I had in mind, Mr. Chairman, when I spoke to the Secretary of State was a matter in connection with the civil service insurance. I desire to ask the minister who is in charge whether any changes have been made since the Auditor General's report of 1953, in volume I at page 33. Under the heading of civil service insurance the Auditor General set the matter out as follows:
There was a year-end balance of $28,382,000 at the credit of the civil service insurance account. Section 15 of the Civil Service Insurance Act requires premiums to be founded on tables "based on the H.M. mortality table of the institute of actuaries of Great Britain, and on a rate of interest of 6 per centum per annum". The statute was enacted 60 years ago and the mortality table employed was published in 1869. The average life expectancy having since considerably lengthened, outlays in the form of payments to beneficiaries have not had the expected impact, a consequence being that the burden on the account is less than the Civil Service Insurance Act anticipated. For this reason, the statutory requirement to use a certain mortality table and the stipulating of a 6 per cent interest rate merit reconsideration.
I should like to ask this question of the Minister of Finance, under whom I understand this matter comes. This report made by the Auditor General on the civil service insurance fund indicates that something should be done, because what he said then was to the effect that by law the mortality table has to be one that was published in 1869. I would ask the minister if that matter has been taken care of?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
May I save my hon. friend time? The scheme was reconsidered. It was discontinued, and has been replaced by the death benefit scheme which we put through this house in the last session.
Supply-Finance
There was no mortality rate table dealt with last session.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall item 113 carry?
No, Mr. Chairman. On what is the mortality rate based now?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: We have not a scheme like that now. We discontinued it.
What is it based on?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: There is not one.
You mean you have an insurance program-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No. We have not an insurance program.
-and there is no basis of mortality rate?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No. We have not an insurance program.
You have not an insurance program?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No. We have superannuation but we have not an insurance program.
How does it tie in?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The very point my hon. friend makes is the one I am making, namely that consequent upon this report and other information this scheme was considered and it was discontinued. It does not exist any more for the reasons referred to, among others.
I have been asked this question about this matter. It is included in what? I do not know the answer. What is the answer?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I do not know how I can make the matter any clearer. There is not any such scheme left. We are not operating the insurance scheme to which my hon. friend refers, for the reasons referred to in that report of the Auditor General.
I may be stupid, but I am going to find out whether I am stupid.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Let me put it this way. We repealed the act to which my hon. friend is referring.
How are you now covered?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: We are not covered at all. It does not exist.
It is now under superannuation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No. We are not writing any more insurance policies since we repealed this act last session, when we put in the death benefits.

Administration of various acts and costs of special functions-
114.	Superannuation and retirement acts, administration, $574,240.

I have a point I wish to raise, and I think it should be raised under item 114. It is in connection with the public service superannuation regulations. I am reading from page 2242, part II of the Canada Gazette of December 22, 1954, and I read as follows:
Notwithstanding anything in this section, a deputy head may, at any time, for reason only of age, terminate the employment of a contributor who has attained 60 years of age, if the deputy head gives to the contributor at least six months notice of termination of employment.
I am puzzled by that regulation. On its face it seems to be an extremely arbitrary power to give. I am particularly puzzled by the part of the phraseology reading "a deputy head may, at any time, for reason only of age". Would the minister please comment on that?

While you are figuring that out, may I ask the minister if he would mind having his staff send me an explanation of this business of the civil service insurance, and in particular what happened to the $28,382,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I shall have a full explanation sent to my hon. friend by the staff.
And what happened to that $28 million?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes.
I am not going to hold up proceedings, but I want to get that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: As to the questions asked by the hon. member for Greenwood, this is a repetition of a section in the former act which means that at or after the age of 60 a civil servant may be invited to take his superannuation by the deputy minister concerned.

Yes, but for reason only of age. I mean is there to be no incapacity to do his work, no disability of any kind? Can the head of a department just say to a man, "You are 62; you are out". Surely that cannot be so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes, that is true, although of course it is not the sort of action that is undertaken unless there are good reasons to do so in the interests of the public service.
Then does the minister not agree that if those are the reasons that are being used-
Would the member for Greenwood speak up a bit? I should like to follow this.
Did my hon. friend hear the clause I read?
No, I did not.

Then I shall read it again.
Notwithstanding anything in this section, a deputy head may, at any time, for reason only of age, terminate the employment of a contributor-
That is a contributor to the superannuation fund.
-who has attained 60 years of age, if the deputy head gives to the contributor at least six months notice of termination of employment.
The minister says, and I find it easy to believe, that this is not acted upon in an arbitrary manner; but does the minister not agree that it is a very odd situation to leave this clause as it stands if the words "for reason only of age" mean, as I think they do, that all the deputy head needs to say to a man is, "You have passed your sixtieth birthday and out you go"? Why is it worded in that way? Is it the natural wording? Did the minister say it was taken from the old act? If it has the practice of many years behind it, that in itself is perhaps some sanction.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am informed the wording is slightly different from the old act but the principle is the same, that at that age there is a discretion in the deputy head. I can only repeat what I have said, and my hon. friend agrees with me, that these actions are not taken without full consideration of the best action in the interests of the public service. My hon. friend might disagree with the regulation and might feel it should be altered. If so I would be glad if he would say so and I will have a look at it, but I think he would agree that at some age, be it 60 or otherwise, there ought to be consideration given to the factors I have mentioned.
Yes and no.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Absolutely, yes and no; no in some cases and yes in others.
I want to submit this to the minister. Am I right in thinking that prima facie a man has the right to go on until he is 65? Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: There is no absolute right to go to 65. Admittedly 65 is the generally accepted age, but there is no right.

That does not seem to me to leave it in a very happy position. I think the minister has said in effect that these actions are not taken purely on the basis of this wording. In other words, I understood him to tell me that it would not

be done by reason only of age between 60 and 65 but that there would have to be some real incapacity to do the job.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: First you must bear in mind that any civil servant may retire at 60, and there is a counterbalance there that he may be retired after 60. But if in the interests of the efficiency of the department the deputy head comes to the conclusion that somebody past 60 might be invited to accept his superannuation, I see no reason why that should not be done in the interests of the service.
Neither do I, but I wish it said that in the section in words very nearly the same as those the minister has just used, instead of saying "for reason only of age".

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: But the difficulty arises that you always have the borderline case where you cannot say to a man that he is not doing his job, but you can say to him if you choose that he is only doing 75 per cent of his job. You do not say that. You say, "Because of age I am asking you to accept your superannuation."

I am not going to take the time of the committee further, but I find it most distasteful. It seems to me it ought not to be worded like that. May I ask the minister if he will have a look at it in the light of this conversation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I will.

I am very glad the hon. member for Greenwood has raised this point. Going home on the bus one night I happened to meet a civil servant who was 62. This provision had just been drawn to his attention, and this man had very important family responsibilities. I think it is unfortunate that the government of Canada as an employer should have a regulation providing that for reason of age only, regardless of the efficiency of the individual, at age 60 an employee is liable to be forced to leave the service. How many have been asked to leave the service under this clause, and will the minister not reconsider the matter in the light of the comments of the hon. member for Greenwood? I think it is a mistake for the government of Canada to assume that there is only a limited amount of work in Canada for all the people to do. Surely people 60, 70 and 75 want to work.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Of course they do, but you do not entrust to some people certain jobs that must be done. There has to be some discretionary right in the deputy head of the department, who is responsible for the efficiency of the department. I am told, though I cannot recall when, that a return was tabled during 50433-4381
Supply-Finance
this session giving the numbers who have been retired under this provision. I have also been told that there have been two in the Department of Finance, so it will be seen how small the numbers are. Nevertheless there may be occasions on which this discretionary right ought to be exercised in the public interest, and that is all.
It is not a matter of great moment. We are not turning many people out who are over 60. In fact I believe the contrary is true. I think the government, certainly from the time the present minister became Minister of Labour, has been encouraging people to continue to work and encouraging employers to ask them to work past 60 and past 65. It has been the policy of the government to employ people and keep them employed. Nevertheless you cannot make an absolute rule about it.

If we are going to have a rule by which people can be thrown out of employment at 60, I submit the minister should bring in legislation to change the Old Age Security Act so that payments will be available at 60. If we are going to make it difficult for people beyond 60 to retain employment in the government service, then such legislation should be introduced.

During the last session of parliament the government introduced legislation setting up a form of life insurance for civil servants and members of the armed forces. In the original bill the government made the insurance compulsory, but I think when the bill reached the other place at the end of the session the compulsory clause was removed and a voluntary condition was introduced but with certain limiting factors. Is provision made under this item for the carrying or financing of that particular insurance scheme? If not, where would the money be found; under what item?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: We can deal with that now if the hon. member wishes to ask a specific question.
I would like to ask a question.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It is a statutory item.

How does that legislation stand, and what is the policy? My recollection is that a canvass was to be made of civil servants and of the armed forces, and if a certain percentage volunteered to accept the conditions, then it was to be made compulsory. If not, the voluntary element would remain; and there was some suggestion- although this was not official at the end of the last session-that action was to be taken between sessions. My recollection was that

Supply-Finance
the scheme would be dropped. I was wondering whether it had been dropped or whether there are funds available here for it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: There is a statutory item making provision for the money. The scheme was not dropped. I made a public announcement when it went into effect. Those covered by the act had until November 1 to opt out. After that date, and after studying the figures of those who had requested not to be covered by the act, we proclaimed it and it has been in operation ever since. I cannot give the exact figure, but I think about 18,000 nonmilitary civil servants elected not to be covered by the act. However, it does apply now to all persons who joined the civil service since that time.
And I understand that the armed services are also included in the act. Can the minister give the committee any information as to how they stand?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: There was a smaller percentage in the armed services who elected not to be covered, but I am not sure of the number. However, I do know that it was a smaller percentage than among civilians.
And those joining the armed forces now have to accept this condition?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes.
Is there any money available to establish that insurance fund?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: A statutory item appears at the bottom of page 23, which deals with the government contribution to the public service death benefit account under part II.

I understood the minister to say to the hon. member for Vancouver East that the government was carrying no insurance plan at all. I recall the situation mentioned by the hon. member who has just spoken, and I thought that was insurance.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: This is a group policy scheme. The hon. member is referring to individual insurance.
But it is still insurance.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes.
You said there was no insurance carried.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No; I said the scheme referred to by the hon. member had been discontinued, and we are no longer writing individual insurance.

Mr. Chairman, in a discussion of the estimate having to do with the administration of the superannuation and retirement acts, could the minister inform the

house whether in the course of his administration any efforts are being devoted to research in connection with a problem raised often by the hon. member for Winnipeg South as well as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.
When a man pays into a superannuation fund plan for a long number of years he is assured of a certain income upon reaching a certain age. This man is making the sacrifice as he goes along, and his sacrifice is tuned to a certain standard of living which will be assured to him when he reaches the age of retirement. I know there are many people in Canada who make great sacrifices over a long number of years to ensure themselves $60, $70 or perhaps $80 a month upon reaching the age of, let us say, 65. However, upon reaching that age they find that in actual standard of living value the thing for which they had been sacrificing so much over all the years has depreciated in value. They find that the purchasing power of their money has been greatly reduced because of the deliberate policy of ministers of finance in the government of Canada, and they have a feeling that somehow or another they have been let down. In a growing nation and an expanding economy I can fully understand why it is in the interests of the nation gradually, over a period of years, to devaluate its currency. Thereby our public debt and carrying charges become much less, and any minister of finance who has heavy public indebtedness on which he has to meet interest rates likes to see a slight inflationary spiral. This inflation helps to ease the load. It lightens the load on anyone who owes money.
Recently the people of Canada went through a period of inflation, and those who owed money did not mind that condition very much. However, it does hit at those who have been making sacrifices for many years to look after themselves in their old age, through superannuation and other plans. I wonder whether the minister's department has been paying any attention to the representations that have been made, particularly those of the hon. member for Winnipeg South, and if so, can we have a report? Is there any way at all in which a superannuation plan operated by the government might be evolved so it would automatically look after inflation and deflation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, if I were able to do that I think I would be the most renowned minister of finance in the world.

Oh, Mr. Chairman, the minister
has not told me whether any attention has been paid to this matter. We have a sum of money set aside here for administration. I would point out to the minister that he and

his predecessors have been responsible for inflation and deflation within our nation. They have a moral obligation to those people who put their savings aside for their old age. If by their actions as ministers of finance they have taken away half the value of that money, then I feel they have an obligation; and the minister has not answered the question satisfactorily.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: To be specific, we are not making a study of what it would cost the taxpayers of Canada to guarantee and pay superannuation in times of inflation at a rate greater than that of the bond; nor are we considering the taking away of benefits of superannuation and pensions in a period of deflation from the person who has a bond.

Mr. Chairman, the minister has made a statement that to the average reader of Hansard may sound reasonable. However, I think I ought to ask whether the minister will not agree that a period of deflation in Canada is just beyond comprehension for many long years to come.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I would be happy to think that the present government could continue for all time the high level of prosperity which it has brought to the Canadian people.

speechtext:
Item agreed to.
115.	The Bank Act-salaries and expenses of the inspector general of banks' office, $31,780.
I want to ask a question about the industrial development bank. I am not quite sure where it comes. Will the minister answer it under this item?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It does not come under any item at all, Mr. Chairman. The industrial development bank is owned by the Bank of Canada and its operations are dealt with in its annual report.

But, Mr. Chairman, may I ask the minister if I am not correct in believing that the Bank of Canada, in some sense anyway, is under the aegis of the Department of Finance? My understanding is that some department is the sponsor or the responsible department for all the crown corporations. Therefore one may ask questions of this type. If that is true of the Bank of Canada, is it not true of the industrial development bank?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The bank of course reports to parliament and I have the honour of tabling the report. If my hon. friend would like to ask a question about the industrial development bank I suggest he do it on the final item of my estimates, but there is no particular item having to do with the bank. I shall be glad to answer any question.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Supply-Finance
116.	Administration of the Farm Improvement Loans Act and the Veterans' Business and Professional Loans Act, $74,178.
Mr. Chairman, I have the report of the Canadian farm loan board before me. I should like to ask the minister a few questions regarding the work of that board.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: This is the Farm Improvement Loans Act. We shall come to the Canadian farm loan board later.
There is no item in the estimates for the Canadian farm loan board.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Ask the question on the final
item.
This item has to do with administration of the office and the cost of special functions. I would presume it is under the Minister of Finance.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I do not object to answering questions, but as I say there is no item for' the farm loan board, just as there is none for the industrial development bank, but I shall answer the questions on the final item of the estimates as I have promised in the other case.

The Farm Improvement
Loans Act is under this item.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is right.
I have before me the annual report in connection with the Farm Improvement Loans Act. The government professes -and I use that word advisedly-to be of help to farmers across this country.
That is right.

I suggest to you, sir, that if you think 5 per cent interest is of much help to farmers then you had better think again, because that is the interest charged under this act and the loan is guaranteed to the bank. I believe the government could do a little better than that. They are guaranteeing the loan to the bank, yet the bank is charging the farmer 5 per cent on that loan. I believe one could go out and get first mortgage loans at 5 per cent almost any place, provided it is on a good mortgage; yet the government says this is a great act for the farmers of Canada.	.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: So it is.

I do not think it is a great act. One has to go to the bank and get money and have the government guarantee the loan to the bank. The bank is not taking any chances. A good farmer can go to the bank and get a loan at 5 per cent without this act at all. He does not need this. It is only on the loans that are questionable; it is only

Supply-Finance
on the risks that are questionable that the bank asks the farmer to come in under the Farm Improvement Loans Act. The banks know they cannot lose the money. I would strongly urge that if the government professes to be helping the farmers, as they say they are, they should lower that interest to at least 4 per cent on these loans. The maximum is $4,000. It is a short-term loan and is used only for building, repairs, implements, and that sort of thing. Surely if it is to be the assistance to the farmers that it is professed to be then the interest should be no more than 4 per cent, if not less than that.
I have some other questions I should like to ask the minister, but I should like to get his reaction to the questions I have just asked.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend proved the case for the Farm Improvement Loans Act by saying that these are marginal loans that the banks would not ordinarily handle. That was the purpose back of the legislation, to assure those persons who were marginal that they would in fact get the loans to assist them in their operations. That is all I can say.
With respect to the interest rate, I shall be glad to look at it to see if it is out of line with normal lending practices at the moment. But bearing in mind that, as my hon. friend said, persons who can get loans anyway would not be borrowing under this act and those who might not will still be borrowing, it is a real advantage to the farmer who gets the loan under these circumstances. It is not insignificant that the total loans under this act have amounted to $513 million. It has been a help to the farmers of Canada despite what my hon. friend may say.
That is true. In effect you are putting a means test on this Farm Improvement Loans Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: All I know is that my hon. friend was in favour of the act when it was passed.

That is very true. What else could we do? We were handed an act and we had to take it or leave it. What I am saying is that by the minister's own admission he is putting a means test on this act, because the farmer who has credit can go to the bank and get money at 5 per cent. The farmer who has not good credit can still go to the bank and get money at 5 per cent and the government guarantees the poor risk. In fact you are putting a means test on this act.
On the back page of the report appear the claims paid by the bank from 1945 to 1954. Altogether there have been 282 claims made and paid by the government to the

banks, amounting to the total of $149,814. Can the minister give me a breakdown of these figures by provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No. All I can give is the breakdown by the various fiscal years. It would take some time to get the information for my hon. friend.
The breakdown by years is here.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is right. If my hon. friend wants to know what provinces they are in I shall be glad to inquire, but it will take some time.
The breakdown of provinces gives almost everything else. We have the provincial breakdown on the amount of the loan and the reason for the loan.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Is the hon. member not content with my promise? I shall get it for you.

This item also covers the Veterans' Business and Professional Loans Act. Is the administration divided between these two acts, or do the same personnel carry out the duties? Is it possible to say how much of this $74,000 odd is allocated to the Veterans' Business and Professional Loans Act and how much to the Farm Improvement Loans Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The staff of the Department of Finance handle this act and do all the work.
Can you tell me, please, whether requests are still being made for loans under this act?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes; 185 loans were made in the fiscal year 1954-55.

I want to get the picture as to whether or not the numbers are decreasing. Is that a rapid decrease or not? There is a general decrease of $12,000 in the cost of administration. That may be explained by the number of applications under the Veterans' Business and Professional Loans Act, and the fact that they are decreasing.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: They were decreasing up to within the last two years, when there was a slight increase by reason of the fact that the veterans of the Korean war are taking advantage of these loans. With that exception, a decrease in the number of applications was beginning to become evident.
These loans are available only to veterans of Korea; the man who is joining the service now would not be eligible?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No.
So we can expect a decrease?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes.

I want to endorse what the hon. member for Brant-Haldimand has said. It is a well recognized fact that the average A-l creditworthy man can borrow money at a bank at 5 per cent, and I think it is ridiculous that the government of Canada should insure the banks against loss when they are lending money at that rate. The other day a minister informed me that the government of Ontario was obtaining money at 3 per cent, so I am sure the government of Canada could get money at a rate lower than 3 per cent. I think the banks could handle these loans at 4 per cent, or even at 3 per cent.
I am not saying this on the spur of the moment, as it is something that has given me some concern of late that the government of Canada should enter the insurance business in connection with loans on National Housing Act homes where the interest rate is 5 per cent and has been even more than that. Not so long ago the banks voluntarily reduced their interest rate by one-half of 1 per cent. That was a most significant move, almost unprecedented. If I had had any money I would have gone out and purchased all the bank shares I possibly could. The banks were making more money than they had anticipated, and the result has been that within the past month bank shares have risen by more than 16 per cent. I think the farmers of Canada would be well served if loans were made under the Farm Improvement Loans Act at 4 or even 3J per cent.
Can the minister indicate when the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act will be proclaimed?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I hope that will be the second thing I will decide after prorogation.

Supply-Finance

That is exactly what I mean. In view of the conditions which existed last year in western Canada I am surprised that this appropriation has been cut. Has the minister any comment to make in that regard?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader

I did promise the person who mentioned it to me in the estimates committee that I would look to see whether because of the conditions that arose in western Canada last year there had been an inclination to refuse loans. I have not been able to find any evidence of that, but I did promise, and I repeat that promise, that I will look to see if that is the case.

I know of numerous occasions where one man who obtained a loan was asked to make his payment in the year he got the loan, while another man was not asked to make his payment until the following year. Are specific instructions given to the banks as to how payments are to be made?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I think my hon. friend will appreciate that it depends largely on when the loan is made. If you borrow money in the spring you will probably be asked to make a payment in the fall, on the assumption that you will have money from your crops. If you borrow money in the fall you probably will not be asked to make a payment until the following crop year. The timing may be fixed at the best time for the borrower to pay.

The minister said he agreed with the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort that generally speaking loans were financed through the Farm Improvement Loans Act. Would he not therefore surmise that the banks are using these facilities when there is no need to do so? In other words, many good risks who normally would be able to go to the bank and get money at 5 per cent are using the facilities of this act, and the banks are simply using the act in the main as added security when they loan money.
The reason I mention this is that in the annual report for the year ending December 31, 1954, there are quite a number of figures as to the extent of the operations of this act. Under the circumstances I think the figures will be misleading. In the main they are not going to reveal the number of marginal loans which will have to be made under this particular act. The figures are misleading in that they include not only those farmers who would have to make use of the facilities

provided by this act, but also all farmers, whether or not they were good risks in the eyes of the banks, who are using the facilities provided under the act.

speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Grants to universities-
126. To provide grants to institutions of higher learning recognized in each province by the government of Canada and the government of the province as being universities or institutions of equivalent standing equal to an amount, for each province, not exceeding 50 cents per head of its population as certified by the dominion bureau of statistics divided among the recognized institutions, of the province proportionately to their enrolment of full time intramural students in personal attendance at the recognized institution or at an institution in the same province affiliated with it who are registered in courses of university level recognized as leading to and counting year for year toward a university degree awarded by a university in Canada and the Minister of Finance may for this purpose more particularly define the terms "university level" and "university degree", $7,800,000.

The university grants have given an impetus and encouragement to the universities the like of which they have certainly never had before in my time. One should congratulate the government for giving and maintaining those, grants. I shall not go into the situation or even discuss the fact that some of those grants are not apparently welcome in certain quarters, because there is a whole constitutional issue in which I do not want to get mixed up at this late date. But it is sure that the increased fees that would be necessarily charged by the universities if these grants were not in existence would preclude the education of many people who are now enjoying such an education owing to the existence of these grants.
The grants make it easier for those with less funds, and I am interested in this angle of the question. They make it easier for those families with less money to spend to send some of their members to university. In that regard it is an excellent piece of social legislation, because it should not be anyone's aim that a university education should be the prerogative of any one class, and when I say "class" I am speaking in terms of money available to the family.
Attendance at university even now, of course, entails sacrifice on the part of members of the family concerned. It is a common fallacy that high school education, for instance, is free to those who are concerned. It is not just a matter of the fact that there are no fees for those people who are attending our high schools, because there are things like food, clothing and transportation which must be taken into consideration. Statistics prove that the amount of money which comes

into the family has a good deal to do with the attendance of high school students and the number of students from a family who can attend the high school.
There is the matter, for instance, of books, and there is the necessity for certain members of the family to work in order to maintain the family income while the other members go to high school. I had the statistics some years ago. It is quite a proven fact that the greater percentage of the children are in the professional classes, followed, I think, by the business classes, followed by skilled labour and unskilled labour in that order.
I am well aware that there are other reasons for that sliding scale, but one of the chief reasons is the amount of income enjoyed or not enjoyed by the families concerned.
While I am speaking on these grants-and I am all in favour of them-I would suggest to the government that they carry their work further by the granting of more scholarships to needy students. We have here an opportunity to mention this in connection with grants to universities. I shall not spend long on this, but I think we need more scholarships. I think the system of grants to university students in Britain has been very successful in this regard. We have had some system of scholarships here, but there has been a tendency to give them for scientific subjects. I suppose one can understand that tendency in times of war or in times of national emergency such as we have had. However, I notice that this government has been much more interested in that type of scholarship than in scholarships for the humanities, which I think are equally necessary, certainly in times of peace. In many families there are clever students who need this type of assistance. The fact that there is a grant to the university as such does not meet their problem.
Of course in my plea for scholarships for the humanities I do not want the scientific subjects to be neglected. It has been noticeable that in Canada most of the scholarships have been in the scientific field, under the influence of defence needs. There is certainly a need for trained personnel particularly in this atomic age. I know there has been difficulty in finding persons to fill certain important posts. I believe it was the Secretary of State who said the other day that there was a shortage of patent engineers and a shortage of engineers in general. I think a system of scholarships, together with the present system of university grants, would improve conditions in that regard.
Supply-Finance
As to the university grants themselves, may I say that I never felt particularly comfortable about the method of their distribution or about the basis upon which they were distributed. It is true that 50 cents per head, if I may put it that way, is a nice easy way of solving the problem. It is easy of administration, but I am not sure that it is completely just. I think need should be taken into consideration; I refer to need in the particular province. I believe that the educational efforts which the province is prepared to make should also be considered. One can easily realize that a province with an extremely large population would not necessarily be as much interested in the education of its young people as would certain other provinces. I think this could be adjusted somehow in order to cover those two matters.
In any case I shall conclude by saying what I rose to say, namely that we are glad of these grants. We are thankful for them. As I say, they have been not only an impetus to the universities and to university education but they have been the very salvation of some of the universities which at present exist but which could not have existed if those grants had not been given. I welcome them as a sign that we are not concerned wholly with material things, though now one might urge, even in the material sense, that a country with such great potentialities and such great natural resources as we have will certainly need skilled minds, if I may put it that way, to administer them and to bring this Canada of ours which has such great potentialities up to the educational level of some of the older but perhaps less fortunate countries of the world in the matter of wealth and natural resources.

There are one or two questions I should like to ask the minister on this item. I assume that the government is guided in its policy decisions by the recommendations made by the Massey commission. On page 355 of its report the commission recommended as follows:
That these contributions-
That is referring to the moneys dealt with in this particular item.
-be sufficient to ensure that the work of the universities of Canada may be carried on in accordance with the needs of the nation.
Since the government set up the commission to make a thorough investigation of the needs of the nation in this respect, I feel that the government is prepared to accept its recommendations as the basis for its policy. I note that the sum of money appropriated under this item is some $7,800,000. I should like to know whether the minister feels that this amount is sufficient to meet the requirement

Supply-Finance
laid down in the recommendation, namely that the appropriation be sufficient to ensure that the work of the universities of Canada may be carried on in accordance with the needs of the nation.
I believe it is generally understood that there are 100,000 university students in Canada. In view of the recommendations made to the commission with regard to what various organizations felt would be a proper form of financial contribution to the universities by the federal government, it seems to me that the amount of this appropriation is clearly insufficient to meet the needs of the nation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: This is the amount recommended by the report from which my hon. friend is reading.
I am not too much concerned with a specific figure. What I am suggesting is this-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: You asked me a question and I answered it by saying that the Massey commission recommended this amount, that being the amount they thought carried out the substance in the report to which he referred.

My question to the minister was whether the government felt it was sufficient. I am dealing with the specific recommendation of the report, namely that appropriations be sufficient to fulfil a certain purpose. I was asking the minister whether it is the view of the government that the sum provided for in this appropriation is sufficient to meet the requirement set out in that recommendation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: My hon. friend bases his appeal to me on the report of the Massey commission. He referred to the government having appointed a commission and having taken some action to adopt as a policy the recommendations made by it. From that I take it or assume that he approves of the report himself and thinks we ought to be carrying it out. In answer to his question, let me say that I take it that this appropriation does carry out what the commission reports.

Might I ask the minister to what year the figure applied which he gave the house a moment ago as being recommended? In what year was that recommendation made? May I ask whether it was the intention of the commission that this should be the amount that should be appropriated each year, or whether it was the start of a program?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
It is in the report itself. It reads as follows:
For example, if the grant were at the rate of fifty cents per head of population-
And so on. I am reading from the report.

That illustrates the very point; "for example." My suggestion is that when the commission made their report they envisaged a long-term approach to this whole problem, and that the figure suggested at that time applied not at this particular moment but at the time the recommendation was made, and was suggested in view of the situation at that time. My contention at this time is that the amount is insufficient. That is the point I want to make to the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I understand that point now. I did not understand that point until this moment.

Irrespective of what recommendation was made by the commission, what I should like to get from the minister is whether in his view the appropriation is sufficient to meet the general requirement laid down in the commission report, namely that the amount of money be sufficient to ensure that the work be carried on in accordance with the needs of the nation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Well, for the third time the answer is yes, but perhaps my hon. friend does not like a forthright yes or no so I shall give him a qualified answer. The recommendation was made by the Massey commission. The government accepted the principle involved in granting moneys to the universities. We conferred with the provincial governments and the universities concerned, or rather with the universities -conference. Certain formulae were worked out. This is the result. After four or five years it is possible my hon. friend may argue that conditions have so changed that the formula no longer applies.
That is my very point.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
All right, I accept my hon. friend's point. It took him a long time to come to it, but we understand each other now. He says we should increase the grant.
I regret that at the moment I only find it possible to recommend this amount to parliament, and that is what I am doing.

I intended to make a few remarks on this item involving grants to universities, but in view of the remarks made by the hon. member for Saskatoon there is little necessity for me to do so. He is widely known, because of his interest in this subject, as more or less the unofficial representative of the universities in this house. With his don-like appearance and logic of Socrates we can leave that subject to him.
However, I do have two questions to ask the minister. What standard is used on which to base the qualifications of a university to

receive these grants, and who compiles the list of universities that are to receive them?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The list has to be approved both by the federal government and the provincial government concerned.
Does each provincial government send a list to the federal government for approval? Is that it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is correct.
On that point, is there not a committee that makes the decision?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: There is a committee that does the work, and it comes through the provincial government concerned.
It is not actually the government that makes the decision.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes, it is.
A committee appointed by the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That may be, but both governments approve the list.

Mr. Chairman, I noted the efforts of the hon. member for Regina City to get the minister to make a statement on whether or not he considered the amount of these payments to be adequate, and the minister expressed his regret that all he was able to recommend was the sum of $7,800,000. I feel that in coming to that decision the minister has possibly ignored some of the other grants he has authorized. I notice that the subsidy to the gold mines, for example, is some $11 million. Surely the minister will agree with me when I propose the idea to him that federal aid to university education is in the long run of far greater significance to the welfare of Canada than is federal aid to the continued operations of gold mines.
I am not opposing subsidies to the gold mines at this time. However, when you look at the amounts we are willing to spend on other things by way of subsidies, the amount of $7,800,000 for the universities is very insignificant indeed. I think we would be making at least a token recognition of the growing importance of university education for our young people if we paid a minimum of $1 rather than 50 cents per head. I doubt very much whether the minister would find much opposition in Canada to that kind of allotment.
For the benefit of members from those parts of Canada which have not yet seen fit to take advantage of these grants, may I say that I come in fairly close contact with the universities in the province of British Columbia, and I have never yet noticed any effort on the part of the minister to exercise 50433-439J
Supply-Finance
any influence on the universities in that province as to the manner in which the educational grant is to be used. In my opinion the resistance to federal grants to universities is based on a false assumption, that assumption being that the federal government will exert an influence on how the grant is to be used by the universities concerned. As far as the University of British Columbia is concerned, I think I can safely say that the grant is being used very directly for the purpose of keeping at a low level the annual fees that have to be paid by the students attending that university.
There is one other reason I should like to advance in my effort to have the minister consider a radical upward revision of these grants at least with respect to the estimates on which he will be working a few months from now. On numerous occasions I have read statements of the Minister of National Health and Welfare addressed to the people of Canada, and have also heard him say that one reason we are unable to have national health insurance is that the technical help is not available in Canada to institute such a program. The other day the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys admitted that he was very short of the trained help he needed in his department. I think almost every minister in the government will agree that he is handicapped in his efforts to obtain necessary civil service personnel by the lack of sufficient adequately trained professional people in the nation. Yet I find that the government is making next to no effort to remedy the situation.
I think the minister will agree with me that for the government to contribute the sum of $7,800,000 in aid of university education in a nation such as Canada is to admit at the same time that the federal government is making next to no effort to aid education at the university level. It may be that seven or eight years ago this amounted to a considerable effort. However, in the light of the cost of education today it is very little indeed.

I hesitate to leave on the record without any challenge the interpretation placed on the recommendation of the Massey commission by the minister. The Massey commission recommendation in this respect is to be found in italics on page 355 of the report. It is true that in section 11 prior to the recommendation the Massey commission does make certain suggestions which the minister has interpreted as being the recommendation. I am going to read the paragraph which the minister has interpreted as the recommendation. It is as follows:
There are a number of ways in which federal aid might be given to universities. We shall

Supply-Finance
recommend that this aid be given but we venture only to suggest how it might be given.
In other words the commission made no attempt to name the amount of money. The report continues:
If a grant were made on the basis of population in each province, it could be distributed among institutions in the province in accordance with the number of students. For example, if the grant were at the rate of fifty cents per head of population, then on the basis of 1949 estimates Manitoba would receive $389,000 which would be divided among the university institutions of Manitoba in accordance with their certified registration.
That is not a recommendation. It is quite clear that the commission was leading up to the recommendation, but they did not recommend 50 cents a head. That' was merely used as an example. Yet the minister has seen fit to lift this example out of context and create the impression that the Massey commission had recommended 50 cents per head as a basis for providing federal aid to universities. What the commission did recommend were four points, and I shall set them out:
(a)	That in addition to the help already being given for research and other purposes the federal government make annual contributions to support the work of the universities on the basis of the population of each of the provinces of Canada.
There again there is no reference at all to any set amount of money. Then they continue:
(b)	That these contributions be made after consultation with the government and the universities of each province, to be distributed to each university proportionately to the student enrolment.
(c)	That these contributions be sufficient to ensure that the work of the universities of Canada may be carried on in accordance with the needs of the nation.
(d)	That all members of the national conference of Canadian universities be eligible for the federal grants mentioned above.
Those are the recommendations of the commission. At no time did the commission recommend a set amount of money. The minister is seeking to justify an inadequate amount provided in this appropriation by referring to the fact that somewhere in the report there was mention of an example-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
May I interrupt the hon. member. He has made his point that he thinks this is inadequate. Now let me make my point, that the presentation made by the conference of universities to the Massey commission worked out to a figure of about $6 million. In working out the recommendation the commission used this figure as an example. That was accepted by the government qs the only stated figure, and was used as its recommendation. If my hon. friend wishes to

say, as he has said, that they did not recommend 50 cents, I agree with him. But this figure was accepted at that time by the government as being a suitable figure, resulting in a grant of over $7,800,000. My hon. friend says this is inadequate; but can we agree that I am prepared to recommend only this amount in the meantime?
My point was to clear up what I believe was a misrepresentation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Then you have done that. I will not accept the word "misrepresentation", but you have cleared it up.
No. This is far too important a subject to be brushed aside arbitrarily. The minister may say that $7 million is all the government of Canada can afford-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I did not say that. Nothing I said could be used to come to that conclusion. I do not want to argue with my hon. friend, because he is making the same point as was made by the hon. member for Regina City, that this grant ought to be increased. I appreciate his argument. I have heard it before, and I am sure on this occasion he has added a certain amount of grace and conviction to it. But at the same time let me point out that I never said I thought the universities of Canada should not have more than $7,800,000.

I still think it is my responsibility as a member to emphasize, with all the force I possibly can, that this aid to universities in Canada by the federal government is utterly inadequate. Today we have hundreds of thousands of boys and girls going to schools manned by inadequately trained teachers. The federal government ought to meet this urgent need of the nation. I have mentioned the field of public health and welfare. While I admit I am not too familiar with that field,
I am familiar with the field of education. And if I had to send my four youngsters either to a public school or a high school and have them supervised by a girl who had only grade 10 education and who was operating under a permit, I know what I would do. Yet that is the situation facing thousands of Canadians at the present time.
The progress of Canada is not forever going to be blocked by the opinion of a few who would like to see this government and all of Canada completely decentralized and become nothing. There is a tendency that has developed within very recent years in the cabinet of Canada. I feel the minister now concerned was not initially responsible; I feel

the Prime Minister shares the major responsibility. If years ago we started paying 50 cents per head for university education, then surely we should have increased that amount by now. We are not making any progress as a national entity. By deliberate design we are moving backward, turning the clock back. For a nation such as Canada to be short of school teachers when it is within the financial power of this government to remedy the situation is a disgrace, and the government must share the blame. For the minister to say we can afford $11 million for the gold mines of Canada and not more than $7 million for education is a disgrace not only to the government but also to the minister who puts forward that idea.
